title: checkout-oom-after-helm-limit-cut
summary: Helm values reduced memory limits for checkout-api from 1Gi to 256Mi. Pods OOMKilled under peak cart traffic; error rate spiked for 18 minutes.
symptoms: OOMKilled, CrashLoopBackOff, 5xx on /checkout
root_cause: memory limit set below real steady-state usage after busy-hour load

title: hpa-maxreplicas-starved-cluster
summary: Helm chart raised HPA maxReplicas for search-api from 10 to 200. Autoscale event during sale caused node pool exhaustion and kubelet pressure cluster-wide.
symptoms: Pending pods, DiskPressure, elevated scheduling latency
root_cause: HPA maxReplicas unbounded relative to cluster capacity
blast_radius: search-api, shared node pool, unrelated namespaces

title: pdb-blocked-node-drain-during-upgrade
summary: New PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable=100% on payments-gateway blocked node drains. Cluster upgrade stalled; old nodes flapped and connection resets rose.
symptoms: drain timeout, Eviction blocked by PDB, elevated TCP resets
root_cause: PDB too strict for rolling node replacement

title: networkpolicy-denied-redis-after-helm-sync
summary: Helm release added default-deny NetworkPolicy without allowing egress to Redis. Orders service could not reach cache; latency and timeouts cascaded.
symptoms: i/o timeout to redis, connection refused from policy drop
root_cause: NetworkPolicy missing egress to Redis CIDR/port

title: image-tag-latest-pulled-breaking-build
summary: Deployment image was :latest. Overnight rebuild of base image broke inventory-worker; CrashLoop after deploy with no chart version change.
symptoms: CrashLoopBackOff, ImportError in startup logs
root_cause: mutable latest tag instead of digest or immutable semver

title: rollingupdate-maxunavailable-too-high
summary: Helm set rollingUpdate maxUnavailable=50% on storefront Deployment. Half the pods terminated at once during release; CDN origin errors during Valentine peak.
symptoms: 503 from ingress, ready replicas dropped sharply
root_cause: aggressive maxUnavailable during high traffic

title: configmap-hot-reload-bad-json
summary: ConfigMap mounted into auth-service updated with invalid JSON feature flags. App hot-reloaded and all pods started failing auth token validation.
symptoms: 401 storm, config parse errors, all replicas unhealthy
root_cause: invalid ConfigMap applied via Helm without schema validation

title: ingress-tls-secret-mismatch
summary: Helm Ingress pointed tls.secretName to rotated secret that was not yet created in namespace. TLS handshake failures for api.example.com.
symptoms: SSL_ERROR, default backend cert served, customer TLS alerts
root_cause: Ingress TLS secret name out of sync with Secret resource

title: initcontainer-wait-for-migrate-hung
summary: Helm chart added initContainer waiting for migrate Job. Job failed silently; new Pods stuck in Init forever; old ReplicaSet scaled down → outage.
symptoms: Pod Initializing forever, Ready=0
root_cause: init dependency on failed Job with no timeout/backoff UX

title: resourcequota-blocked-new-pods
summary: Namespace ResourceQuota CPU was lowered via Helm umbrella chart. Deployments could not schedule new pods during rollout; old pods terminated first.
symptoms: forbidden: exceeded quota, Deployment progress deadline
root_cause: ResourceQuota too low for surge pods during RollingUpdate

title: servicemonitor-scrape-storm
summary: Helm values enabled ServiceMonitor with 5s scrape and huge metric cardinality for checkout. Prometheus memory ballooned; alert evaluation delayed.
symptoms: Prometheus OOM, rule evaluation lag, missing alerts
root_cause: high-cardinality metrics + aggressive scrape interval

title: helm-hook-pre-upgrade-deleted-pvc-data
summary: pre-upgrade Helm hook Job ran a cleanup that deleted PVCs labeled app=analytics. StatefulSet lost volumes; dashboards blank after upgrade.
symptoms: PVC Terminating, empty PersistentVolume claims, data loss
root_cause: destructive Helm hook without dry-run guard

title: nodeaffinity-pinned-to-draining-pool
summary: Deployment required nodeAffinity to gpu-spot pool. Spot interruption drained nodes; pods could not reschedule elsewhere; inference API down.
symptoms: Pending Unschedulable, spot interruption events
root_cause: hard affinity to interruptible pool without fallback

title: sidecar-injection-cpu-throttle
summary: Istio sidecar injection enabled via Helm label change. Sidecar default CPU limits starved app containers; p99 latency tripled.
symptoms: CPU throttling, high p99, envoy proxy busy
root_cause: sidecar resource defaults not tuned for latency-critical service

title: cronjob-concurrency-policy-forbid-backlog
summary: CronJob concurrencyPolicy=Forbid with long-running job. Missed schedules piled up; when job finished, manual catch-up overloaded DB.
symptoms: missed CronJob schedules, DB connection spikes later
root_cause: Forbid + long runtime without monitoring missed runs

title: liveness-probe-too-aggressive-after-chart-change
summary: Helm lowered liveness probe timeoutSeconds and period. Slow JVM warmup caused kubelet to kill pods repeatedly during rollout.
symptoms: Liveness probe failed, restart thrash, rollout stuck
root_cause: liveness probe tighter than startup characteristics

title: horizontal-pod-disruption-during-vpa-update
summary: VPA in updateMode=Auto resized recommendations mid-traffic. Pods restarted en masse; recommendation service flapped.
symptoms: mass restarts, InPlaceOrRecreate events, error budget burn
root_cause: VPA Auto mode on latency-sensitive Deployment

title: service-selector-mismatch-after-label-rename
summary: Helm chart renamed pod labels but Service selector not updated. Endpoints emptied; notifications silently dropped.
symptoms: Endpoints empty, Service no pods, traffic blackhole
root_cause: label selector drift between Service and Pod template

title: UPGRADE FAILED: No resource with the name "" found
summary: ## Repro Create a simple Chart.yaml: ``` yaml name: upgrade-repro version: 0.1.0 ``` With a single K8S resource in the `templates/` dir: ``` yaml kind: ConfigMap apiVersion: v1 metadata: name: cm1 data: example.property.1: hello ``` Install the chart: ``` bash helm install . exasperated-op Last Deployed: Tue Sep 13 12:43:23 2016 Namespace: default Status: DEPLOYED Resources: ==> v1/ConfigMap NAME DATA AGE cm1 1 0s ``` Verify the release exists: ``` bash helm status exasperated-op Last Deployed:…
symptoms: ## Repro Create a simple Chart.yaml: ``` yaml name: upgrade-repro version: 0.1.0 ``` With a single K8S resource in the `templates/` dir: ``` yaml kind: ConfigMap apiVersion: v1 metadata: name: cm1 data: example.property.1: hello ``` Install the chart: ``` bash helm install . exasperated-op Last Deployed: Tue Sep 13 12:43:23 2016 Namespace: default Status: DEPLOYED Resources: ==> v1/ConfigMap NAME DATA AGE cm1 1 0s ``` Verify the release exists: ``` bash helm status exasperated-op Last Deployed: Tue Sep 13 12:43:23 2016 Namespace: default Status: DEPLOYED Resources: ==> v1/ConfigMap NAME DATA AGE cm1 1 1m ``` Now add a 2nd K8S resource in `templates/` dir: ``` yaml kind: ConfigMap apiVersion: v1 metadata: name: cm2 data: example.property.2: hello ``` Upgrade the chart: ``` bash helm upgrade exasperated-op . Error: UPGRADE FAILED: Looks like there are no changes for cm1 ``` That's weird. Bump the version in Chart.yaml: ``` yaml name: upgrade-repro version: 0.2.0 ``` Try upgrade again: ``` yaml helm upgrade exasperated-op . Error: UPGRADE FAILED: No resource with the name cm2 found. ``` ## Expected `helm upgrade` should create the `cm2` resource instead of erroring that it doesn't exist. Edit: to be clear: helm _is_ creating the `cm2` ConfigMap, but helm fails regardless. ## Current state after performing steps ``` bash helm status exasperated-op Last Deployed: Tue Sep 13 12:43:23 2016 Namespace: default Status: DEPLOYED Resources: ==> v1/ConfigMap NAME DATA AGE cm1 1 6m kubectl get configmap --namespace default NAME DATA AGE cm1 1 6m cm2 1 4m ```
root_cause: this happens because when helm is determining what has changed it looks for the *new* configmap resource in the *old* release, and fails to find it. See https://github.com/kubernetes/helm/blob/master/pkg/kube/client.go#L276-L280 for the code where this error comes from. Tiller logs for the failing upgrade:

title: gzip: invalid header
summary: I'm getting "gzip: invalid header" from helm/tiller when trying to install a chart from a helm repository hosted through[ bitbucket.io](https://confluence.atlassian.com/bitbucket/publishing-a-website-on-bitbucket-cloud-221449776.html). I've also tried an Azure CDN and get the same error. These are the basic build steps for installing helm and packaging the chart. At the end I simply add the .tgz and updated index to a repository and commit it. It seems like when the file is fetched/downloaded u…
symptoms: I'm getting "gzip: invalid header" from helm/tiller when trying to install a chart from a helm repository hosted through[ bitbucket.io](https://confluence.atlassian.com/bitbucket/publishing-a-website-on-bitbucket-cloud-221449776.html). I've also tried an Azure CDN and get the same error. These are the basic build steps for installing helm and packaging the chart. At the end I simply add the .tgz and updated index to a repository and commit it. It seems like when the file is fetched/downloaded using helm the gzip compression is stripped off and we are left with a tar file, however if I just use a browser to download the file the gzip compression is left intact and we can install that file local from disk just fine. What am I doing wrong/How do I fix this? ```
root_cause: that Atlassian decompressed on the server (on upload), and rather than re-compressing when they serve or serving as a different mime type they simply serve the decompressed file as if it was compressed. This causes the error observed above. You can see error explained in [`BCLOUD-21555`](https://jira.atlassian.com/browse/BCLOUD-21555?jql=project%20in%20(BCLOUD%2C%20BSERV)%20AND%20text%20~%20%22gzip%20bitbucket%22%20ORDER%20BY%20cf%5B13230%5D%20ASC) the best. Except there the problem pertains to images not helm charts. Also it's not just Helm that's broken on BitBucket, apparently all of Chrome is. I would **not** have set `DisableCompression` to true. The problem is that Atlassian mistakenly marks files they intentionally decompress as compressed. It's in their court.

title: Tiller causing Kubelet to leak memory
summary: The node that is running Tiller causes the Kubelet to leak memory. Depending on how frequently Tiller is polled by the Helm client, influences how much memory is leaked. This has been verified on 3 different clusters running Kubernetes 1.6.8. Talking to other users, we have identified this problem also existing with 1.5.x, 1.7.x and 1.8.x clusters. On a cluster where Helm commands were being issued 20 times per minute (over 100 releases), in a period of a day we caused the Kubelet to consume ov…
symptoms: The node that is running Tiller causes the Kubelet to leak memory. Depending on how frequently Tiller is polled by the Helm client, influences how much memory is leaked. This has been verified on 3 different clusters running Kubernetes 1.6.8. Talking to other users, we have identified this problem also existing with 1.5.x, 1.7.x and 1.8.x clusters. On a cluster where Helm commands were being issued 20 times per minute (over 100 releases), in a period of a day we caused the Kubelet to consume over 70GB of memory. ``` PID USER PR NI VIRT RES SHR S %CPU %MEM TIME+ COMMAND 13268 root 20 0 78.295g 4.521g 48336 S 24.6 30.3 12:53.83 kubelet ``` Further investigation identified an extremely large number of `socat` processes running on the node (over 1000). Here is a sample of the process list. ``` root 27500 0.0 0.0 21740 2976 ? S 07:52 0:00 /usr/bin/socat - TCP4:localhost:44134 root 27501 0.0 0.0 21740 3004 ? S 07:52 0:00 /usr/bin/socat - TCP4:localhost:44134 root 27502 0.0 0.0 21740 3004 ? S 07:52 0:00 /usr/bin/socat - TCP4:localhost:44134 root 27503 0.0 0.0 21740 2920 ? S 07:52 0:00 /usr/bin/socat - TCP4:localhost:44134 root 27504 0.0 0.0 21740 2812 ? S 07:52 0:00 /usr/bin/socat - TCP4:localhost:44134 root 27505 0.0 0.0 21740 2976 ? S 07:52 0:00 /usr/bin/socat - TCP4:localhost:44134 ``` I reached out to @justinsb who verified this on a 1.8.x cluster on a fresh installation of Helm. Justin found the likely cause of the problem being the following block of code (and comment explaining the edge case). https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/master/pkg/kubelet/dockershim/docker_streaming.go#L191-L192 ``` // If we use Stdin, command.Run() won't return until the goroutine that's copying // from stream finishes. Unfortunately, if you have a client like telnet connected // via port forwarding, as long as the user's telnet client is connected to the user's // local listener that port forwarding sets up, the telnet session never exits. This // means that even if socat has…
root_cause: caused by the kubelet itself leaking memory on port forwarding requests. It _should_ be reproducible by merely creating and destroying a few thousand port-forwards with `kubectl`. But it does appear to be beyond our ability to fix in Tiller code, since it's a bug in the kubelet. If anyone can reproduce with just `kubectl`, we should open an upstream bug.

summary: Output of `helm version`: ``` Client: &version.Version{SemVer:"v2.8.2", GitCommit:"a80231648a1473929271764b920a8e346f6de844", GitTreeState:"clean"} Server: &version.Version{SemVer:"v2.8.2", GitCommit:"a80231648a1473929271764b920a8e346f6de844", GitTreeState:"clean"} ``` Output of `kubectl version`: ``` Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"10", GitVersion:"v1.10.0", GitCommit:"fc32d2f3698e36b93322a3465f63a14e9f0eaead", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2018-03-26T16:55:54Z", GoVersion:"g…
symptoms: Output of `helm version`: ``` Client: &version.Version{SemVer:"v2.8.2", GitCommit:"a80231648a1473929271764b920a8e346f6de844", GitTreeState:"clean"} Server: &version.Version{SemVer:"v2.8.2", GitCommit:"a80231648a1473929271764b920a8e346f6de844", GitTreeState:"clean"} ``` Output of `kubectl version`: ``` Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"10", GitVersion:"v1.10.0", GitCommit:"fc32d2f3698e36b93322a3465f63a14e9f0eaead", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2018-03-26T16:55:54Z", GoVersion:"go1.9.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"} Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"10", GitVersion:"v1.10.0", GitCommit:"fc32d2f3698e36b93322a3465f63a14e9f0eaead", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2018-03-26T16:44:10Z", GoVersion:"go1.9.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} ``` Cloud Provider/Platform (AKS, GKE, Minikube etc.): **Minikube** **Description**: When running `helm fetch` or `helm install` to install/fetch a specific versioned chart using `--version=` option, helm CLI doesnt respect the passed version to `--version` and instead always installs latest one. In other words, `--version=` is not working as expected. This was tested where charts were uploaded to chartmuseum. **Steps To Reproduce** 1. Start a local chartmuseum server: ``` docker run \ -d \ --name chartmuseum \ -p 8088:8080 \ -e STORAGE="local" \ -e STORAGE_LOCAL_ROOTDIR="./chartstorage" \ chartmuseum/chartmuseum ``` 2. Create a simple helm chart `my-app` ``` helm create my-app ``` 3. Package the chart with one version: ``` helm package my-app/ --version=1.0.0-dev1+1 ``` 4. Package same chart again with different version: ``` helm package my-app/ --version=1.0.0-dev1+2 ``` 5. Upload both charts to local chartmuseum ``` curl --data-binary "@my-app-1.0.0-dev1+2.tgz" http://localhost:8088/api/charts curl --data-binary "@my-app-1.0.0-dev1+1.tgz" http://localhost:8088/api/charts ``` 6. Add the chartmuseum as helm repo: ``` helm repo add cmtest http://localhost:8088/ ``` 7. Refresh the indexes:…
root_cause: caused by an misinterpretation of the the Semver specification which states that > Build metadata SHOULD be ignored when determining version precedence. Thus two versions that differ only in the build metadata, have the same precedence.

title: During `helm upgrade`, Tiller chooses the wrong current revision to generate patches from when the previous upgrade failed
summary: I typed up a long test rapport to find and reproduce the issue, so I'll just copy-paste the relevant stuff here. I had 4 test cases in total, and case 3 turned out to be the one that reproduces the issue.
symptoms: I typed up a long test rapport to find and reproduce the issue, so I'll just copy-paste the relevant stuff here. I had 4 test cases in total, and case 3 turned out to be the one that reproduces the issue.
root_cause: Tiller actually does not apply complete manifests to Kubernetes, but uses a Kubernetes library to build patches based on a previous revision. symptoms: We've seem to have encountered either a regression in `v2.12.0` or at least some behaviour that was recently changed. Our values file contains the following: ```yaml some_key: ``` And we're using those values in our environment variables: ```yaml env: - name: SOME_KEY value: {{ .Values.some_key | quote }} ``` In `v2.11.0` this would evaluate to: ```yaml - name: SOME_KEY value: ``` In `v2.12.0` however it shows the following diff if we upgrade our helm deployments: ```diff - name: SOME_KEY - value: + value: "<nil>" ``` This is causing quite a few of our deployments to fail since we're trying to pass the string `"<nil>"` as a configuration option instead of an empty string value. Is this a bug or a new feature where empty values are interpreted as `<nil>`? Output of `helm version`: ``` Client: &version.Version{SemVer:"v2.11.0", GitCommit:"2e55dbe1fdb5fdb96b75ff144a339489417b146b", GitTreeState:"clean"} Server: &version.Version{SemVer:"v2.12.0", GitCommit:"d325d2a9c179b33af1a024cdb5a4472b6288016a", GitTreeState:"clean"} ``` Output of `kubectl version`: ``` Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"10", GitVersion:"v1.10.7", GitCommit:"0c38c362511b20a098d7cd855f1314dad92c2780", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2018-08-20T10:09:03Z", GoVersion:"go1.9.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"} Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"11+", GitVersion:"v1.11.2-gke.18", GitCommit:"5796233393d7bc034428de15191ad3d2eaff95fb", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2018-11-08T20:49:08Z", GoVersion:"go1.10.3b4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} ``` Cloud Provider/Platform (AKS, GKE, Minikube etc.): GKE
root_cause: caused by a change in Go 1.11, where untyped nil values are now passed in to template functions when using the text/template package as described [here](https://golang.org/doc/go1.11#text/template). Unfortunately, some of the template functions in the sprig library are not expecting nil values and that is why you are seeing the `"<nil>"` output. I think this needs to be fixed in sprig, and I have a PR that at least addresses this for some of the string functions https://github.com/Masterminds/sprig/pull/133.

title: --kubeconfig flag is ignored
summary: Hi, the --kubeconfig flag is ignored in the helm3 alpha2 release. Best regards, Tobi Output of `helm version`: version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.0.0-alpha.2", GitCommit:"97e7461e41455e58d89b4d7d192fed5352001d44", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.12.7"}
symptoms: Hi, the --kubeconfig flag is ignored in the helm3 alpha2 release. Best regards, Tobi Output of `helm version`: version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.0.0-alpha.2", GitCommit:"97e7461e41455e58d89b4d7d192fed5352001d44", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.12.7"}
root_cause: The problem is that helm passes all of `os.Args` to this `Parse` function, however that particular `FlagSet` only has the flags added during the call to `settings.AddFlags(flags)`. This causes an error because the parse function will find the `-i` flag, not recognize it, and error out, leaving the remaining flags unparsed. Helm silently ignores the error and continues onward, potentially failing later on. The solution lies in the `ParseErrorsWhitelist.UnkownFlags` of the Persistent flags. The PR that implements this solution is here: https://github.com/helm/helm/pull/6076

symptoms: I'm doing some work on a Kubernetes controller that deploys Helm charts to multiple remote clusters through a CRD. Regularly, I'd have this controller reconcile the Custom Resources concurrently, but there's a race condition caused by concurrent writes to scheme.Scheme. Taking a look at `kube.New` today: https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/5c592dcca685b3e5887e3c241bb2a73a43191f62/pkg/kube/client.go#L62 The call to `AddToScheme`, behind the scenes appends to a slice. This means that attempting to call AddToScheme concurrently can cause a panic. The good news is, because that scheme.Scheme is globally available, we only need to add the CRD types once, no matter how many Kube clients we need to create. So, I'd like to propose perhaps wrapping that AddToScheme in a `sync.Once` or something of that nature. I understand that mine is a pretty specific use case, and I'd be happy to contribute any fixes for making Helm more controller-friendly. Thanks!
root_cause: caused by concurrent writes to scheme.Scheme. Taking a look at `kube.New` today: https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/5c592dcca685b3e5887e3c241bb2a73a43191f62/pkg/kube/client.go#L62

title: bug(pkg/repo/index): --merge flag misbehaves on valid SemVer 2 versions

But, when this index --merge is done with a valid SemVer 2 version such as `0.1.0-alpha.1+001.asdf1234` in one file, and `0.1.0-alpha.1` in the other, they instead override each other in either direction.

But, when this index --merge is done with a valid SemVer 2 version such as `0.1.0-alpha.1+001.asdf1234` in one file, and `0.1.0-alpha.1` in the other, they instead override each other in either direction.
root_cause: caused by the shared logic within masterminds/semver library. I think there is an assumption that it will differentiate between versions, but it considers `0.1.0+mybuild` the same as `0.1.0` I think. I reported an issue in masterminds/semver about the behavior that leads to this that I certainly consider a bug for helm. I'm not sure if it is considered a bug within masterminds/semver though. https://github.com/Masterminds/semver/issues/137

symptoms: ## Error when installing large charts ### Encountered Error After upgrading Helm, when I attempt to install a large chart (~400 resources), Helm exits with an error. Before the upgrade, an install on the same chart worked without errors. The new error is: (Redacted full hostname, namespace and deployment name): ``` Error: rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists. Unable to continue with install: could not get information about the resource: Get "https://<redacted>.eks.amazonaws.com/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/<redacted>/deployments/<redacted>": dial tcp: lookup <redacted>.eks.amazonaws.com: no such host ``` This error happens after around ~250 _successful_ calls to the EKS cluster (when validating resources). It always dies on the validation for this **specific** resource (which does not exist, it's a clean cluster). ### Error Source > Note: I am not a seasoned Go vet, nor am I well versed in the lower level C/CGO DNS implementation, nor do I know much about file system and file descriptors. The following is the result of some digging, but my understanding might very well be incorrect...! Looking into this error, it turns out the error is poorly reported; the resource does _not_ exist in the EKS cluster, and the host _is_ reachable - there are successful requests between client <> server up until this error is encountered. The encountered error stems from a golang built-in source [`net/cgo_unix.go#L177`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/net/cgo_unix.go#L177) and is raised as `EAI_NONAME`. When this type is encountered, Golang returns `err = errNoSuchHost`. This error type is a known misnomer (as described in [`net/lookup_unix.go#L331`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/net/lookup_unix.go#L331)) when encountered on some systems, including Darwin (MacOS). After more investigation into this, it turns out that the error is raised when the system runs out of file descriptors which are used when making DNS requests with the C implement…
root_cause: that too many requests are being made concurrently (or at least too quickly) by Helm, resulting in running out of file descriptors. On one hand, a revert in the imported `client-go` library to re-introduce caching would solve this, but my guess is that the removal of caching for certain transport types is intentional and good design.

title: Helm runs out of memory parsing large index.yaml files
summary: I have access to two privately hosted Helm repos that I was recently attempting to pull Helm charts from. For some reason, only for one of the repos, the _helm_ binary would crash due to a lack of memory whenever I tried the following command: `helm repo update` -- I even tried removing the repo and re-adding it (`helm repo add`) but I ran into the same issue: Specifically, _helm_ would fail with this error message: `fatal error: runtime: out of memory`. This was for version `3.2.1` of _helm_.…
symptoms: I have access to two privately hosted Helm repos that I was recently attempting to pull Helm charts from. For some reason, only for one of the repos, the _helm_ binary would crash due to a lack of memory whenever I tried the following command: `helm repo update` -- I even tried removing the repo and re-adding it (`helm repo add`) but I ran into the same issue: Specifically, _helm_ would fail with this error message: `fatal error: runtime: out of memory`. This was for version `3.2.1` of _helm_. I then moved to a brand new machine to see if I could replicate this error. On that machine, I installed the latest version of Helm (`3.6.2`). I got similar behaviour: Only for that one repo, _helm_ would crash, but now the error message was different: `Killed` Eventually though, after running the same `helm repo add` command multiple times, I guess I got lucky and the command completed. In the process though, _helm_ generated a MASSIVE amount of warning messages that looked like this: ``` index.go:339: skipping loading invalid entry for chart "..." "..." from ...: validation: chart.metadata.version "..." is invalid ``` This message appears to be generated when Helm checks the chart versions for SemVer compliance, as per [this security notice](https://github.com/helm/helm/security/advisories/GHSA-c38g-469g-cmgx). Since the repo that kept causing _helm_ to run out of memory is also the one with apparently a massive amount of charts with noncompliant versions, **it seems like the Helm validation is inadvertently causing the memory issues -- i.e. since our Helm repo has so many noncompliant charts, _helm_ runs out of memory, and I am unable to even add that repo.** Unfortunately, I do not own/control the repo, so is there any way we can mitigate this performance hit on the Helm side? Perhaps a flag to the _helm_ binary that tells it not to generate a separate warning message for every single noncompliant chart? ps: The only confusing thing is that I saw this memory error on two…
root_cause: caused by the volume of warning messages, then I suspect that PR would solve this issue as well. @mattfarina @bacongobbler Would appreciate your thoughts on this issue and the linked PR when you get a chance!

title: helm failed to resolve on osx when cgo_enabled false
summary: Hi guys, after https://github.com/helm/helm/commit/3490f1e7b6d76709b7ea195370f7db463735f9e2#diff-76ed074a9305c04054cdebb9e9aad2d818052b07091de1f20cad0bbac34ffb52R80 helm stopped working with osx `/etc/resolver/*` files. It was very useful in case of corporate VPN dns resolving. https://github.com/golang/go/issues/12524 ``` > helm list --all Error: Kubernetes cluster unreachable: Get "https://<k8s_server>:8443/k8s/clusters/c-pkq2n/version": dial tcp: lookup <k8s_server> on <external_dns_instead_…
symptoms: Hi guys, after https://github.com/helm/helm/commit/3490f1e7b6d76709b7ea195370f7db463735f9e2#diff-76ed074a9305c04054cdebb9e9aad2d818052b07091de1f20cad0bbac34ffb52R80 helm stopped working with osx `/etc/resolver/*` files. It was very useful in case of corporate VPN dns resolving. https://github.com/golang/go/issues/12524 ``` > helm list --all Error: Kubernetes cluster unreachable: Get "https://<k8s_server>:8443/k8s/clusters/c-pkq2n/version": dial tcp: lookup <k8s_server> on <external_dns_instead_of_corporate>:53: no such host ``` Output of `helm version`: `version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.8.2", GitCommit:"6e3701edea09e5d55a8ca2aae03a68917630e91b", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.18.1"}` Output of `kubectl version`: ``` Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23", GitVersion:"v1.23.5", GitCommit:"c285e781331a3785a7f436042c65c5641ce8a9e9", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-03-16T15:51:05Z", GoVersion:"go1.17.8", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/amd64"} Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"20", GitVersion:"v1.20.8", GitCommit:"5575935422cc1cf5169dfc8847cb587aa47bac5a", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2021-06-16T12:53:07Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.13", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} WARNING: version difference between client (1.23) and server (1.20) exceeds the supported minor version skew of +/-1 ``` Also I've found that os x binaries on https://github.com/helm/helm/releases are built with build-cross make target (as far I can guess) which differ from `helm install` binary.
root_cause: caused by us forcing `CGO_ENABLED=0` in commit https://github.com/helm/helm/commit/3490f1e7b6d76709b7ea195370f7db463735f9e2 (released in helm 3.8.2). To fix this, we either need to expose a method of setting `CGO_ENABLED=1` in our [`make build`](https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/bed23120b048977d67c929cec915e1d6e0887c5d/Makefile#L79-L80) or revert `CGO_ENABLED` to be `1` by default (as it was for helm 3.8.1 and before).

System Preferences -> Network -> Advanced -> DNS

symptoms: I currently have a very strange behaviour, where helm template shows different annotations, than what is deployed in the cluster afterwards. I provided an example code here <https://github.com/BlacCello/helm-template-bug>. You can see the issue when: 1. root_cause: caused by the Kubernetes cluster. I run `helm upgrade --install -n test --create-namespace test . --debug`, with the --debug flag so that I could see the YAML generated by Helm. title: Invalid helm charts are not fully excluded in helm search result
summary: I have an umbrella helm chart with two dependencies with the same sub-chart, identified by alias. However, my helm repository (powered by JFrog) fails to record the alias in its metadata. Helm 3.14.0 starts to enforce on this kind of metadata (via https://github.com/helm/helm/pull/9176), so my umbrella helm charts become "invalid" now, and helm reported below error message: index.go:366: skipping loading invalid entry for chart "some-chart" "some-version" from <dir_name>helm-index.yaml: validat…
symptoms: I have an umbrella helm chart with two dependencies with the same sub-chart, identified by alias. However, my helm repository (powered by JFrog) fails to record the alias in its metadata. Helm 3.14.0 starts to enforce on this kind of metadata (via https://github.com/helm/helm/pull/9176), so my umbrella helm charts become "invalid" now, and helm reported below error message: index.go:366: skipping loading invalid entry for chart "some-chart" "some-version" from <dir_name>helm-index.yaml: validation: **more than one dependency with name or alias** "sub-chart-name" While the repository metadata needs to record aliases to make it compatible with new helm rules, on the other hand, I find helm may return some of these invalid helm charts back in the search result. After my troubleshooting, I located below code as the root cause: pkg/repo/index.go ``` // loadIndex loads an index file and does minimal validity checking. // // The source parameter is only used for logging. // This will fail if API Version is not set (ErrNoAPIVersion) or if the unmarshal fails. func loadIndex(data []byte, source string) (*IndexFile, error) { i := &IndexFile{} if len(data) == 0 { return i, ErrEmptyIndexYaml } if err := jsonOrYamlUnmarshal(data, i); err != nil { return i, err } for name, cvs := range i.Entries { for idx := len(cvs) - 1; idx >= 0; idx-- { if cvs[idx] == nil { log.Printf("skipping loading invalid entry for chart %q from %s: empty entry", name, source) continue } if cvs[idx].APIVersion == "" { cvs[idx].APIVersion = chart.APIVersionV1 } if err := cvs[idx].Validate(); err != nil { log.Printf("skipping loading invalid entry for chart %q %q from %s: %s", name, cvs[idx].Version, source, err) cvs = append(cvs[:idx], cvs[idx+1:]...) } } } i.SortEntries() if i.APIVersion == "" { return i, ErrNoAPIVersion } return i, nil } ``` To be specific, it is this line: `cvs = append(cvs[:idx], cvs[idx+1:]...)` This slice operation removed items from cvs, ideally, it should remove corresponding item…

symptoms: With Helm `v3.14.0` the following use case is broken: ``` dependencies: - name: kube-rbac-proxy version: "0.9.1" repository: "<redacted>" alias: loki-query-proxy condition: loki-query-proxy.enabled - name: kube-rbac-proxy version: "0.9.1" repository: "<redacted>" alias: loki-ingestion-proxy condition: loki-ingestion-proxy.enabled ``` Various Helm commands (e.g. `helm dependency update`) now lead to the following error message: `index.go:366: skipping loading invalid entry for chart "<redacted>" "1.3.0" from <redacted>: validation: more than one dependency with name or alias "kube-rbac-proxy"` According to the [documentation for the Chart.yaml](https://helm.sh/docs/topics/charts/#the-chartyaml-file) using name twice with separate aliases seems to be valid: > alias: (optional) Alias to be used for the chart. Useful when you have to add the same chart multiple times The error was probably introduced with [this PR](https://github.com/helm/helm/pull/9176). With Helm `v3.13.2` it worked without any problems.
root_cause: caused by JFrog Artifactory as my chart repository. Artifactory removes the `alias` attributes for indexing. In Artifactory the repository index.yaml (which gets downloaded and cached by Helm) contains these dependencies, which are now invalid: ```yaml dependencies: - name: kube-rbac-proxy version: "0.9.1" repository: "<redacted>" - name: kube-rbac-proxy version: "0.9.1" repository: "<redacted>" ```

symptoms: When invoking an `Install` or `Upgrade` action via the API with an array value passed as a typed object, the validation fails with: ``` test-chart: - at '/dummies': invalid jsonType []map[string]interface {} ``` This happens if the array was given as a Go array-of-objects (`[]map[string]any`): ``` _, err = installAction.Run(chart, map[string]any{ // Use of map[string]any (array-of-objects) causes validation to fail! "dummies": []map[string]any{ { "foo": 1, "bar": "test-value", }, }, }) ``` If I convert the dummies array into an untyped array (`[]any`) first, then validation passes as expected: ``` _, err = installAction2.Run(chart, map[string]any{ // Here, dummies is an untyped array of any, and now validation succeeds. "dummies": []any{ map[string]any{ "foo": 1, "bar": "test-value", }, }, }) ``` I believe this happens because v3.18.5 switched the JSON validation library, which is stricter about the types that it accepts. Specifically, the implementation of its `typeOf()` only accepts untyped arrays (`[]any`), but not arrays that have a stronger type specified. See here: https://github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/blob/32784e992ee32ae73891b165b1319dd0bca87437/schema.go#L128

symptoms: Helm 4's `helm template` command defaults to Kubernetes 1.20 instead of matching the client-go version (currently 1.34). This causes charts that use `.Capabilities.KubeVersion` to render old/deprecated API versions. Charts using capability detection (like Bitnami's common library) render `policy/v1beta1` instead of `policy/v1` for PodDisruptionBudgets, `batch/v1beta1` instead of `batch/v1` for CronJobs, etc. **Root cause:** The `Makefile` (lines 70-71) has incorrect LDFLAGS paths. title: helm uninstall --wait misses some resources
summary: Looks like `helm uninstall --wait` doesn't actually wait for all resources. I've noticed that when programmatically running a delete action followed immediately by `kubectl delete ns <namespace>`. When running the two commands in succession (e.g. in a script), namespace deletion takes more than **2 minutes**. When adding `sleep 5` between the two commands, namespace deletion takes **a couple of seconds**. When the namespace is stuck in "Terminating", I can see the following resources in the nam…
symptoms: Looks like `helm uninstall --wait` doesn't actually wait for all resources. I've noticed that when programmatically running a delete action followed immediately by `kubectl delete ns <namespace>`. When running the two commands in succession (e.g. in a script), namespace deletion takes more than **2 minutes**. When adding `sleep 5` between the two commands, namespace deletion takes **a couple of seconds**. When the namespace is stuck in "Terminating", I can see the following resources in the namespace: ``` NAME HOLDER AGE lease.coordination.k8s.io/ingress-nginx-leader ingress-nginx-controller-6c657c6487-vcdcl 28s NAME SECRETS AGE serviceaccount/default 0 59s NAME DATA AGE configmap/kube-root-ca.crt 1 59s NAME TYPE DATA AGE secret/ingress-nginx-admission Opaque 3 42s ``` **However**, removing these resources doesn't resolve the finalizer, and in the "good" case (sleeping for 5 seconds before deletion) the namespace is removed quickly despite these resources existing in it so it doesn't seem like any of these specific resources is the culprit. It seems to me like the `--wait` operation returns too early, thus causing a race condition with any subsequent commands, although I'm not sure which resources it is missing. Maybe it's an _ordering_ problem? Or something to do with webhooks?
root_cause: I can simply set `DeletionPropagation` to `foreground` in the `Uninstall` action (`pkg/action/uninstall.go`) in my code which fixes the problem there, too. I'll leave it to you to decide whether it's worth changing the default for library consumers, too.

title: isMatchingInfo compares full GVK causing resource deletion when API version changes
summary: When upgrading a Helm release where a custom resource changes API version (e.g., from `v2beta1` to `v2beta2` of the same CRD), Helm 4 incorrectly treats the old and new versions as **different resources**. This causes it to **delete the old version** (which is the same underlying object in etcd) after creating the new version, effectively deleting the resource that was just created. The wait then times out because the resource no longer exists: ``` timeout waiting for: [CrdUpgradeTestb/default/…
symptoms: When upgrading a Helm release where a custom resource changes API version (e.g., from `v2beta1` to `v2beta2` of the same CRD), Helm 4 incorrectly treats the old and new versions as **different resources**. This causes it to **delete the old version** (which is the same underlying object in etcd) after creating the new version, effectively deleting the resource that was just created. The wait then times out because the resource no longer exists: ``` timeout waiting for: [CrdUpgradeTestb/default/b status: 'NotFound'] ```
root_cause: In https://github.com/helm/helm/pull/12581, `isMatchingInfo` in `pkg/kube/resource.go` was changed from comparing **Kind + Group** (ignoring Version) to comparing the **full `GroupVersionKind` struct** (including Version): ```go // Before (Helm 3.x): func isMatchingInfo(a, b *resource.Info) bool { return a.Name == b.Name && a.Namespace == b.Namespace && a.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Kind == b.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Kind && a.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Group == b.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Group } // After (Helm 4): func isMatchingInfo(a, b *resource.Info) bool { return a.Name == b.Name && a.Namespace == b.Namespace && a.Mapping.GroupVersionKind == b.Mapping.GroupVersionKind } ``` This means that when a resource changes API version (e.g., `crd-upgrades.example.com/v2beta1` → `crd-upgrades.example.com/v2beta2`), `Difference()` considers them as non-matching. Helm's `update()` method then: 1. **Creates/updates** the new version (`v2beta2`) of the resource 2. Computes `originals.Difference(targets)` — the old version (`v2beta1`) is in the difference set because it doesn't match the new version 3. **Deletes** the old version — but since both versions share the same underlying storage in the Kubernetes API server, this deletes the resource that was just created in step 1 4. The resource is now gone, and the wait times out with `NotFound`

title: Regression from Helm 3: annotateAndMerge corrupts manifests when rendered template content has --- followed by no newline
summary: Hi team! When a chart template has `---` followed by `{{- include ... }}` (note the `{{-` which trims whitespace), the Go template `{{-` directive trims the newline after `---`, producing `---apiVersion: v1\n...` as the raw rendered content. This can happen at the start of a template file or between documents in a multi-document template. In Helm v4, the new `annotateAndMerge()` function in `pkg/action/action.go` parses this content with `kio.ParseAll()` before sending it to post-renderers. `ki…
symptoms: Hi team! When a chart template has `---` followed by `{{- include ... }}` (note the `{{-` which trims whitespace), the Go template `{{-` directive trims the newline after `---`, producing `---apiVersion: v1\n...` as the raw rendered content. This can happen at the start of a template file or between documents in a multi-document template. In Helm v4, the new `annotateAndMerge()` function in `pkg/action/action.go` parses this content with `kio.ParseAll()` before sending it to post-renderers. `kio.ParseAll()` correctly (per the YAML spec) interprets `---apiVersion` as a YAML mapping key — not a document separator followed by a mapping — and then re-serializes it as `'---apiVersion': v1`. This corrupts the manifest — the resource loses its `apiVersion` field entirely. The bug only triggers when a `PostRenderer` is set (since `annotateAndMerge` is only called in the `if pr != nil` branch). The Helm CLI doesn't use a post-renderer by default, which is why `helm install` and `helm template` work fine. However, the Helm SDK is used by projects like [Flux helm-controller](https://github.com/fluxcd/helm-controller), which always sets a PostRenderer to inject origin labels — causing all such charts to fail. Related issue: https://github.com/fluxcd/helm-controller/issues/1423
root_cause: `pkg/action/action.go`: ```go func annotateAndMerge(files map[string]string) (string, error) { // ... for _, fname := range fnames { content := files[fname] // ... manifests, err := kio.ParseAll(content) // <-- parses raw rendered template if err != nil { return "", fmt.Errorf("parsing %s: %w", fname, err) } // ... } // ... } ``` The rendered template content for a file like: ```yaml --- {{- include "mychart.service" . }} ``` After Go template execution is: ``` ---apiVersion: v1 kind: Service ... ``` `kio.ParseAll()` does not recognize `---apiVersion` as a YAML document separator followed by content. Instead, it parses it as a YAML mapping key `---apiVersion` with value `v1`, and re-serializes it as `'---apiVersion': v1`. This also affects multi-document templates where `---` appears between documents: ``` {{ include "lib.deployment" (list . "mychart.deployment") }} {{ define "mychart.deployment" }} {{ end }} --- {{- include "lib.service" (list . "mychart.service") }} {{ define "mychart.service" }} {{ end }} ``` Here the `---\n{{-` in the middle of the file produces the same `---apiVersion` corruption for the service document.

title: kube: IsReachable panics on second call when client creation fails (typed-nil cached in getKubeClient)
summary: I use Helm as a Go package (`helm.sh/helm/v4` v4.2.0), not the CLI. `kube.(*Client).IsReachable()` panics with a nil pointer dereference when it is called a second time on a `Client` whose Kubernetes client could not be created on the first call. The root cause is in `getKubeClient`: ```go func (c *Client) getKubeClient() (kubernetes.Interface, error) { var err error if c.kubeClient == nil { c.kubeClient, err = c.Factory.KubernetesClientSet() } return c.kubeClient, err } ``` `KubernetesClientSe…
symptoms: I use Helm as a Go package (`helm.sh/helm/v4` v4.2.0), not the CLI. `kube.(*Client).IsReachable()` panics with a nil pointer dereference when it is called a second time on a `Client` whose Kubernetes client could not be created on the first call. The root cause is in `getKubeClient`: ```go func (c *Client) getKubeClient() (kubernetes.Interface, error) { var err error if c.kubeClient == nil { c.kubeClient, err = c.Factory.KubernetesClientSet() } return c.kubeClient, err } ``` `KubernetesClientSet()` returns `(*kubernetes.Clientset, error)`. When `ToRESTConfig()` fails (for example, the selected context does not exist, or the config is empty), it returns `(nil, err)`. The `nil` concrete pointer is then stored into the `c.kubeClient` field, which is an interface (`kubernetes.Interface`). A typed nil stored in an interface makes the interface itself non-nil. Because of this: 1. First call to `getKubeClient`: `c.kubeClient` is nil, so it calls the factory. The factory returns `(nil, err)`. The field now holds a typed nil, and the error is returned. `IsReachable` sees the error and returns a clean "kubernetes cluster unreachable" error. This part is fine. 2. Second call to `getKubeClient`: `c.kubeClient == nil` is now false (the interface is non-nil), so the factory is not called again. It returns the typed-nil client and `err == nil`. 3. Back in `IsReachable`, both error checks pass because the error is nil. The code then runs `client.Discovery().ServerVersion()`. `Discovery()` on the nil `*Clientset` returns nil, and the call to `ServerVersion()` panics. This is easy to hit through the action package, because more than one action checks reachability on the same `Configuration.KubeClient`. For example, a common install flow first runs `history` (which calls `IsReachable`) and then `install` (which also calls `IsReachable`). The first check returns the error, but the second check panics instead of returning the same error. This is not a caller-side problem. I only use th…
root_cause: in `getKubeClient`: ```go func (c *Client) getKubeClient() (kubernetes.Interface, error) { var err error if c.kubeClient == nil { c.kubeClient, err = c.Factory.KubernetesClientSet() } return c.kubeClient, err } ```

title: `--wait` hangs for the full timeout on fast resource deletions in v4.2.1 (regression from v4.2.0)
summary: After upgrading from Helm v4.2.0 to v4.2.1, any `helm upgrade --install --wait` that deletes a resource and waits for it to be gone sits there for the entire `--timeout` instead of returning as soon as the resource is actually deleted. It does not error out. After the full timeout elapses it just continues and the release reports success. So an install that used to take a couple of minutes now takes 10+ minutes per deletion wait, but still exits 0. I hit this with hook resources that use `helm.…
symptoms: After upgrading from Helm v4.2.0 to v4.2.1, any `helm upgrade --install --wait` that deletes a resource and waits for it to be gone sits there for the entire `--timeout` instead of returning as soon as the resource is actually deleted. It does not error out. After the full timeout elapses it just continues and the release reports success. So an install that used to take a couple of minutes now takes 10+ minutes per deletion wait, but still exits 0. I hit this with hook resources that use `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation`. On each upgrade Helm deletes the old hook object and waits for it to disappear before recreating it. The object is gone almost immediately, but the wait runs the full clock.
root_cause: This looks like a side effect of #32081 (merged May 30, shipped in v4.2.1), which changed `WaitForDelete` / `statusObserver` in the `kube` package. That PR was fixing a flaky test: during informer sync, resources briefly show as `Unknown`, and the old observer would cancel the watch too early on that, causing intermittent timeouts in the full test suite. The fix defers the early-cancel decision when every resource is `Unknown` and nothing has a definitive status yet, and it treats "timeout while everything is `Unknown` or `NotFound`" as not-an-error. The problem is that a quick deletion looks exactly like that case. The resource really is gone, but the watcher reports `Unknown`/`NotFound` during sync, so the new logic defers instead of recognizing the deletion and waits until the context deadline (the `--timeout`). When the deadline hits with everything `NotFound`, it is treated as success rather than failure, which is why the wait silently eats the full timeout and then continues. So it fixed a premature-exit race in tests and introduced a delayed-exit latency bug in real deletions. v4.2.0 exited in ~0.1s, v4.2.1 waits the entire timeout.

title: Helm v4 silently ignores a values file when the final unterminated line length is a multiple of 4096 bytes
summary: Helm v4 appears to silently ignore a valid values document when its final logical line does not end with a newline, and has a byte length that is an exact multiple of 4096. This is reproducible with compact, single-line JSON files passed through -f/--values. In Helm v4.x, a values file is read and passed to loader.LoadValues, and loader.LoadValues constructs a Kubernetes YAMLReader over Go's default buffered reader: pkg/chart/v2/loader/load.go: ```go func LoadValues(data io.Reader) (map[string]…
symptoms: Helm v4 appears to silently ignore a valid values document when its final logical line does not end with a newline, and has a byte length that is an exact multiple of 4096. This is reproducible with compact, single-line JSON files passed through -f/--values. In Helm v4.x, a values file is read and passed to loader.LoadValues, and loader.LoadValues constructs a Kubernetes YAMLReader over Go's default buffered reader: pkg/chart/v2/loader/load.go: ```go func LoadValues(data io.Reader) (map[string]any, error) { values := map[string]any{} reader := utilyaml.NewYAMLReader(bufio.NewReader(data)) for { currentMap := map[string]any{} raw, err := reader.Read() if err != nil { if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) { break } return nil, fmt.Errorf("error reading yaml document: %w", err) } if err := yaml.Unmarshal(raw, &currentMap); err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("cannot unmarshal yaml document: %w", err) } values = MergeMaps(values, currentMap) } return values, nil } ``` Go's bufio.NewReader uses a default buffer size of 4096 bytes. The underlying issue appears to be in the interaction between LineReader.Read() and YAMLReader.Read() in Kubernetes apimachinery: kubernetes/apimachinery v0.36.0 pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go: ```go func NewYAMLReader(r *bufio.Reader) *YAMLReader { return &YAMLReader{ reader: &LineReader{reader: r}, } } ``` ```go func (r *LineReader) Read() ([]byte, error) { var ( isPrefix bool = true err error line []byte buffer bytes.Buffer ) for isPrefix && err == nil { line, isPrefix, err = r.reader.ReadLine() buffer.Write(line) } buffer.WriteByte('\n') return buffer.Bytes(), err } ``` LineReader.Read() accumulates fragments returned by bufio.Reader.ReadLine() and may return the completed final line together with io.EOF. However, YAMLReader.Read() checks io.EOF before appending the line returned by that call to its own document buffer: ```go line, err := r.reader.Read() if err == io.EOF { if buffer.Len() != 0 { return buffer.Bytes(), nil } return nil, err } buffer.Write(li…
root_cause: The underlying issue appears to be in the interaction between LineReader.Read() and YAMLReader.Read() in Kubernetes apimachinery: kubernetes/apimachinery v0.36.0 pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go: ```go func NewYAMLReader(r *bufio.Reader) *YAMLReader { return &YAMLReader{ reader: &LineReader{reader: r}, } } ```

host: test.netingress.com http: paths: - backend: serviceName: ingressapp servicePort: 80 path: / tls: - hosts: - test.netingress.com secretName: aaa.netingress.v1 ``` **What happened**: For https rule, nginx gets a wrong src ip or "real ip": 127.0.0.1. nginx log: ``` 127.0.0.1 - [127.0.0.1] - - [17/Jan/2020:08:19:39 +0000] "GET / HTTP/2.0" 200 468 "-" "curl/7.54.0" 30 0.001…
root_cause: when enable-ssl-passthrough, ingress-nginx processes https packets on port 443 firstly, then passes it to nginx via proxy protocol. nginx does not get the client ip from proxy protocol, but from IP packets. So the "src ip" is always 127.0.0.1.

symptoms: **NGINX Ingress controller version**: 0.30.0 **Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): v1.15.9-gke.24 **Environment**: - **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: GKE **What happened**: I noticed cert authorities to be invalid, but only for a (few) second (chrome automatically retries). **How to reproduce it**: Not sure, but I have seen the issue several times. This time I managed to find the cause of the issue. The only thing I noticed in the logs just before the failure were 2 instances of `upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream`. This might be a coincidence, but it might have cause the crash of the nginx master (see below), as this was caused by an application bug(now fixed, using a lot of memory) causing that upstream server to be OOMKilled by Kubernetes several times. ** other **: - browsers often keep connections open when they are valid, so the issue wasn't that clear, except on 1/3 of the new connections made (3 replicas) - easier test was to use: `openssl s_client -showcerts -servername <dns-name> -connect <ip/dns-name>:443` multiple times, example(truncated) output of 2 runs: ``` 5:01 CONNECTED(00000003) depth=2 O = Digital Signature Trust Co., CN = DST Root CA X3 verify return:1 depth=1 C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = Let's Encrypt Authority X3 verify return:1 depth=0 CN = <dns-name> verify return:1 --- 5:01 depth=0 O = Acme Co, CN = Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate verify return:1 depth=0 O = Acme Co, CN = Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate verify error:num=21:unable to verify the first certificate verify return:1 ``` - Nginx log, other 2 instances were fine: ``` 2020/05/19 16:24:52 [error] 189#189: *3836424 upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream 2020/05/19 16:25:42 [error] 189#189: *3836424 upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream…

symptoms: **NGINX Ingress controller version**: 0.44.0 **Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): 1.18.3 **Environment**: - AWS - Debian 10.8 - Linux 5.4.96 - Weave-net 2.6.5 **What happened**: We encountered a major production outage a few days ago that was traced back to ingress-nginx. ingress-nginx pod logs were filled with messages like the following: ``` 2021/02/22 22:30:18 [alert] 27#27: worker process 38 exited on signal 11 (core dumped) ``` We discovered that the following message was being printed to the system log as well (timed with the worker exits): ``` Feb 22 22:30:18 ip-10-153-47-170 kernel: traps: nginx[24701] general protection fault ip:7f03278adc59 sp:7ffcdba0aa10 error:0 in ld-musl-x86_64.so.1[7f032789f000+48000] ``` I ultimately identified that whatever was occurring was linked to the version of ingress-nginx we were using and reverted production to 0.43.0 until we could identify the underlying issue. We have a few other lower-load ingress-nginx deployments that have remained at 0.44.0 and have observed apparently random worker crashes however there are always enough running workers and these are infrequent enough that things seemingly remain stable. I was able to get a worker coredump from one of those infrequent crashes and the backtrace is as follows: ``` Core was generated by `nginx: worker process is shutting down '. Program terminated with signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault. #0 a_crash () at ./arch/x86_64/atomic_arch.h:108 108 ./arch/x86_64/atomic_arch.h: No such file or directory. [Current thread is 1 (LWP 38)] (gdb) backtrace #0 a_crash () at ./arch/x86_64/atomic_arch.h:108 #1 get_nominal_size (end=0x7f03273ee90c "", p=0x7f03273ec4d0 "") at src/malloc/mallocng/meta.h:169 #2 __libc_free (p=0x7f03273ec4d0) at src/malloc/mallocng/free.c:110 #3 0x00007f0327811f7b in lj_vm_ffi_call () from /usr/local/lib/libluajit-5.1.so.2 #4 0x00007f0327858077 in lj_ccall_func (L=<optimized out>, cd=<optimized out>) at lj_ccall.c:1382 #5 0x00007f032786e38d in lj_…
root_cause: caused by the base image upgrade (alpine 3.13) but we have seen the same issue as well in our environment after upgrading to 0.44.0. It had happened for 4 times in two days before we downgraded to 0.43.0. We haven't seen a single instance after the downgrade. All 4 incidents were started with nginx config reload

symptoms: **NGINX Ingress controller version**: v1.0.0 **Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): v1.20.9 **Environment**: Bare Metal **What happened**: Before v1.0.0, there's a check to skip validating ingress with a different ingressclass: https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/blob/f3c50698d98299b1a61f83cb6c4bb7de0b71fb4b/internal/ingress/controller/controller.go#L224 In v1.0.0, this code is removed. With multiple ingress controllers, both will validate the same ingress. If we create two ingresses with same host and path but different ingressclasses, the second one will be rejected. **What you expected to happen**: skip validating ingress with a different ingressclass /kind bug
root_cause: The problem is that the validation webhook enabled for the two cluster wide ingress controllers also tries to validate the ingress objects created for this third legacy controller. If I turn off the validation webhook in the two cluster wide controllers all the three ingress controllers works as expected, and they are only picking up ingress objects with the correct class, regardless of the ingress class name being defined in annotations or using the spec.ingressClassName field.

In the past the session cookie was completely ignored by the canary, which means even if the user was already affinitized to a primary pod, using the header defined by canary-by-header or the cookie defined by canary-by-cookie, the user would go to the canary side. As we use the canary feature mainly for internal testing, and additionally for selected users(we set the cookie for them), we depended on this behavior. With the new release using affinity-canary-behavior: "legacy", if the user is already affinitized to a primary pod, it will completely ignore the canary header/cookie, until the session cookie is deleted/ expired, which is a breaking change for us, as it now requires manual deletion of the session cookie, to direct the user to the canary side. **What you expected to happen**: Using the affinity-canary-behavior: "legacy", restores the old behavior when the session cookie was completely ignored by the canary feature, so with the correct canary header/cookie the user goes to the canary side even if already affinitized to a primary pod. symptoms: **What happened**: My enviroment is: clinet->F5->K8s ingress-nginx->server Sometimes HTTP 502 occurs. Since both the F5 and ingress-nginx access logs lack the corresponding records, I believe the 502 error was not caused by a server anomaly. I noticed that the time difference between the occurrence and the ingress-nginx log entry “NGINX load triggered due to a change in configuration” is always within 3 seconds. By actively modifying any ingress to trigger an nginx reload, I was indeed able to reproduce the issue with some probability. By capturing packets on the F5 side and periodically collecting Conntrack information on the ingress nodes, I observed the following information: i) A persistent connection is maintained between F5 and the K8s ingress-nginx, and the connection where the 502 error occurred remains active. ii) At 16:51:19.220, ingress-nginx logs “Backend successfully reloaded.” iii) At 16:51:19.221, ingress-nginx logs type: ‘Normal’ reason: ‘RELOAD’ NGINX reload triggered due to a change in configuration. iv) At 16:51:20.368, ingress-nginx responds to a request from F5 on this connection with a status code 200. v) At 16:51:20.518, F5 sends a POST request to ingress-nginx using this connection. vi) At 16:51:20.525, ingress-nginx responds to this request with an RST packet. vii)Conntrack information shows that at 16:51:19, this connection was in the ESTABLISHED state, and at 16:51:20, this connection was in the CLOSE state. **What you expected to happen**: ingress-nginx responds without RST. ingress-nginx responded with an RST. **NGINX Ingress controller version** (exec into the pod and run `/nginx-ingress-controller --version`): NGINX Ingress controller Release: v1.1.1 Build: a17181e43ec85534a6fea968d95d019c5a4bc8cf Repository: https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx nginx version: nginx/1.19.9 **Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): (Openshift Container Platform)Server Version: 4.12.55 Kubernetes Version: v1.25.16+bd92d70 **Environment**: -…

symptoms: **What happened**: We set `ssl-session-tickets` and `ssl-session-ticket-key` in configmap so the SSL session resumption starts working through session tickets. We saw this error in log > E0718 20:13:57.087788 5 store.go:731] unexpected error writing ssl-session-ticket-key to /etc/nginx/tickets.key: open /etc/nginx/tickets.key: permission denied The file that should be created for ticket key does not exists. **What you expected to happen**: Ticket key from config map will be written to the file `/etc/ingress-controller/tickets.key` **NGINX Ingress controller version** 1.11.3 **Kubernetes version** 1.30.4 **How to reproduce this issue**: set `ssl-session-tickets = true` and `ssl-session-ticket-key = <some key>` in configmap **Anything else we need to know**: I think issue was created here https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/commit/9ed0d7f7afa3e6deaf88ee5b7d787abe26da9229#diff-5f4da05f4716a8d567db533819486a784e3f4993c11021da3b569564c78a5935R1218 because here the path to tickets.key is changed to new folder, but that same folder is then here https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/commit/9ed0d7f7afa3e6deaf88ee5b7d787abe26da9229#diff-9695be8f0aac1e548a5ecec853de2cd6d7d3d1f70e9fd2d735a59449aeedd259L52 removed so the www-data user cannot write key from configmap to the file. Maybe author intended to use folder `/etc/ingress-controller/ssl` ? I think the problem is that container user www-data is trying to write ticket key to file in folder `/etc/ingress-controller/` but because of removing that folder from the list, www-data is not owner of that folder anymore and cannot write the file here.
root_cause: the problem is that container user www-data is trying to write ticket key to file in folder `/etc/ingress-controller/` but because of removing that folder from the list, www-data is not owner of that folder anymore and cannot write the file here.

title: Ingress nginx completely broken for Akamai since 1.13.2 - 403 errors
summary: **What happened**: We upgraded our nginx ingress controller from 1.12.0 to 1.13.2 and now all requests coming via Akamai are denied with a 403 error. **What you expected to happen**: In Akamai we have enabled "Origin IP Access Control List" - this means that traffic from akamai hits our ingress from one of the known Akamai IPs. The Client IP is additionally sent in an extra header called True-client-ip Our ingress configs have an IP whitelist set for the Akamai IPs. This is how we force all tra…
symptoms: **What happened**: We upgraded our nginx ingress controller from 1.12.0 to 1.13.2 and now all requests coming via Akamai are denied with a 403 error. **What you expected to happen**: In Akamai we have enabled "Origin IP Access Control List" - this means that traffic from akamai hits our ingress from one of the known Akamai IPs. The Client IP is additionally sent in an extra header called True-client-ip Our ingress configs have an IP whitelist set for the Akamai IPs. This is how we force all traffic to go via akamai and prevent anyone going direct to our origin. The problem is that since 1.31.2 we are now seeing the actual client IP and not the Akamai IP and are therefore blocking it. We should be seeing the Akamai IP and therefore allowing the traffic **NGINX Ingress controller version** (exec into the pod and run `/nginx-ingress-controller --version`): ``` NGINX Ingress controller Release: v1.13.2 Build: 11c69a64ce3c5bdfb6782434d9f62296d4b42179 Repository: https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx nginx version: nginx/1.27.1 ``` **Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): Server Version: v1.32.7-eks-b707fbb **Environment**: - **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: - **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): Bottlerocket OS 1.43.0 (aws-k8s-1.32) - **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): 6.1.141 - **Install tools**: EKS - **How was the ingress-nginx-controller installed**: ArgoCD, using the helm chart sources: - https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx version: 4.13.2 **How to reproduce this issue**: Deploy the ingress nginx controller with the following config options set: ``` allow-snippet-annotations: 'true' annotations-risk-level: Critical enable-underscores-in-headers: "true" server-tokens: "false" use-forwarded-headers: "false" proxy-real-ip-cidr: List of Akamai IP Ranges use-proxy-protocol: "true" use-gzip: "true" ssl-session-tickets: "true" ``` An ingress config like this: ``` apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: origin-mydomain-ing…
root_cause: The problem is that since 1.31.2 we are now seeing the actual client IP and not the Akamai IP and are therefore blocking it. We should be seeing the Akamai IP and therefore allowing the traffic

summary: **What happened**: The Admission Validation logic (`checkOverlap`) incorrectly skips checking subsequent Rules and Paths if the **first** Rule/Path in the Ingress definition is valid (no conflict). This allows an Ingress with conflicting rules to bypass the admission controller and be successfully applied to the cluster, as long as the conflicting rule is placed **after** a non-conflicting rule in the YAML definition. symptoms: **What happened**: The Admission Validation logic (`checkOverlap`) incorrectly skips checking subsequent Rules and Paths if the **first** Rule/Path in the Ingress definition is valid (no conflict). This allows an Ingress with conflicting rules to bypass the admission controller and be successfully applied to the cluster, as long as the conflicting rule is placed **after** a non-conflicting rule in the YAML definition. Specifically, in `internal/ingress/controller/controller.go`, inside the `checkOverlap` function, there is a `return nil` statement inside the inner Path loop. This causes the function to exit immediately after verifying the first path of the first rule, ignoring all remaining paths and rules. **What you expected to happen**: The Admission Controller should check **ALL** rules and paths defined in an Ingress object for conflicts. If **any** rule/path conflicts with an existing Ingress, the request should be rejected, regardless of the order of rules in the YAML. **NGINX Ingress controller version**: Latest (and affects previous versions as well). Code logic issue exists in `main` branch. **Kubernetes version**: All versions. **Environment**: - **Cloud provider**: Any (Logic issue) - **OS**: Any - **Install tools**: Any **How to reproduce this issue**: 1. **Create a Victim Ingress (A)** that occupies a specific host/path. apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: victim namespace: default spec: ingressClassName: nginx rules: - host: conflict.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: http-svc port: number: 80 2. **Create an Intruder Ingress (B)**. **Crucial Step**: Define a **non-conflicting** rule FIRST, and the **conflicting** rule SECOND. apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: intruder namespace: default spec: ingressClassName: nginx rules: # Rule 1: No conflict (Safe) - host: safe.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: http-svc port: n…

This looks like using the wrong mergeKey, and indeed the code backs that up: 2508 type ServiceSpec st…
symptoms: User reported: I am running a service with both TCP and UDP: ``` spec: type: NodePort ports: - protocol: UDP port: 30420 nodePort: 30420 - protocol: TCP port: 30420 nodePort: 30420 ``` but kubectl describe service shows only UDP. ``` Type: NodePort IP: 10.0.13.152 Port: <unset> 30420/UDP NodePort: <unset> 30420/UDP Endpoints: 10.244.4.49:30420 ``` When I change the order then it shows only TCP. This looks like using the wrong mergeKey, and indeed the code backs that up: 2508 type ServiceSpec struct { 2509 // The list of ports that are exposed by this service. 2510 // More info: http://kubernetes.io/docs/user-guide/services#virtual-ips-and-service-proxies 2511 Ports []ServicePort `json:"ports,omitempty" patchStrategy:"merge" patchMergeKey:"port" protobuf:"bytes,1,rep,name=ports"` The key should probably be "name", though that can be empty if there is a single port only - is that a problem? @ymqytw ?
root_cause: caused by the bug of using the wrong json pkg in the api server (#42488). It has been fixed by #42489. issues with ports: - [x] #42488 number conversion issue caused by using the wrong json pkg. - [ ] (this issue) mergeKey for ports (port #) is not unique. The ports will still be PATCHed wrongly if the user does something like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/39188#issue-197312716

title: In IPVS mode, host services become available on ClusterIPs
summary: **What happened**: In IPVS mode, if a service on the host is listening on `0.0.0.0:<some port>`, pods on the local host (or incoming traffic from other hosts if routing allows it) to any ClusterIP on `<some port>` reaches the host service. For example, a pod can access its host's ssh service at something like `10.96.0.1:22` **What you expected to happen**: ClusterIPs should reject or drop traffic to unexpected ports (as is the behaviour in iptables mode). **How to reproduce it (as minimally and…
symptoms: **What happened**: In IPVS mode, if a service on the host is listening on `0.0.0.0:<some port>`, pods on the local host (or incoming traffic from other hosts if routing allows it) to any ClusterIP on `<some port>` reaches the host service. For example, a pod can access its host's ssh service at something like `10.96.0.1:22` **What you expected to happen**: ClusterIPs should reject or drop traffic to unexpected ports (as is the behaviour in iptables mode). **How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**: - Turn on IPVS mode for kube-proxy - Configure ssh to listen on 0.0.0.0 (the default in most installations) - Exec into a pod and ssh to, say `10.96.0.1:22`, should reach the host. **Anything else we need to know?**: This unexpected behaviour has some security impact; it's an extra, unexpected, way for packets to reach the host. In addition, it's very hard for a NetworkPolicy provider to secure this path (such as Calico) to secure this path because IPVS captures traffic that, to the kernel's policy engines, looks like it's going to be terminated at the host. For example, in iptables, there's no way to tell the difference between traffic that is about to be terminated by IPVS and traffic that's going to go to a local service. Related Calico issue; user was trying to block the traffic with Calico policy but was unable to (because Calico has to whitelist all potential IPVS traffic): https://github.com/projectcalico/calico/issues/2279 **Environment**: - Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.12 - Cloud provider or hardware configuration: - OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): - Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): - Install tools: - Others: /kind bug
root_cause: we bind ClusterIP to `kube-ipvs0` interface in the host. However, if we don't bind the ClusterIP to the interface, IPVS won't work. I am not sure if we can drop the packets?

title: kube-proxy ipvs conn_reuse_mode setting causes errors with high load from single client
summary: **What happened**: The kube-proxy sets `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/vs/conn_reuse_mode` to zero https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go#L340 This has the effect that when: - kube-proxy uses ipvs mode and an ipvs virtualserver is configured with only a few realservers (pod replicas) - a client sends a lot of requests so that the source ports are reused before the MLS expires - a pod gets removed(e.g. via upgrade) removed while it receives traffic from this client Wh…
symptoms: **What happened**: The kube-proxy sets `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/vs/conn_reuse_mode` to zero https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go#L340 This has the effect that when: - kube-proxy uses ipvs mode and an ipvs virtualserver is configured with only a few realservers (pod replicas) - a client sends a lot of requests so that the source ports are reused before the MLS expires - a pod gets removed(e.g. via upgrade) removed while it receives traffic from this client What happens in this situation is that the kube-proxy correctly sets the wait of the realserver to 0 and creates a new realserver with for the new pod that replaces the removed pod. The problem is that the kube-proxy will not remove the weight zero realserver until its connections drop to zero. This will never happen as the `conn_reuse_mode` is set to 0 and the client reuses its source ports. This causes the kernel to constantly reuse connections and send the traffic to the weight 0 realserver. **What you expected to happen**: When the old pod is removed its realserver receives no traffic anymore and is removed by kube-proxy **How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**: Deploy a service with with only a few replica pods as endpoints. start sending lots of traffic to that service from a single client so the client will reuse its source ports sooner than the maximum segment lifetime of tcp connections. For example with fortio: ``` fortio load -t 0 -qps 1000 -c 16 -keepalive=0 http://10.86.6.96 ``` delete a pod on the node. Fortio will now produce following errors occassionally: ``` 08:50:10 E http_client.go:558> Unable to connect to 10.86.6.96:80 : dial tcp 10.86.6.96:80: connect: no route to host 08:50:11 E http_client.go:558> Unable to connect to 10.86.6.96:80 : dial tcp 10.86.6.96:80: connect: no route to host 08:50:12 E http_client.go:558> Unable to connect to 10.86.6.96:80 : dial tcp 10.86.6.96:80: connect: no route to host 08:50:13 E http_client.go:558>…
root_cause: The problem is that the kube-proxy will not remove the weight zero realserver until its connections drop to zero. This will never happen as the `conn_reuse_mode` is set to 0 and the client reuses its source ports. This causes the kernel to constantly reuse connections and send the traffic to the weight 0 realserver. **What you expected to happen**: When the old pod is removed its realserver receives no traffic anymore and is removed by kube-proxy

root_cause: caused by the directory already existing and not by an actual problem creating it. The code could check before returning the error.

title: Short running pods take very long to teardown
summary: In master we continue to see instances of short running pods failing to terminate quickly, due to races between sources of truth. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102025#issuecomment-843622820 stops e2e tests from "cheating" and bypassing kubelet shutdown, and as a result some tests fail predictably (garbage collection lots of short running pods for testing various behaviors). The linked comment shows a pod that is racing between container start and pod delete. The problem is that…
symptoms: In master we continue to see instances of short running pods failing to terminate quickly, due to races between sources of truth. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102025#issuecomment-843622820 stops e2e tests from "cheating" and bypassing kubelet shutdown, and as a result some tests fail predictably (garbage collection lots of short running pods for testing various behaviors). The linked comment shows a pod that is racing between container start and pod delete. The problem is that dispatchWork invokes `podAndContainersAreTerminal()` on the containerstart event, but the cache that `podAndContainersAreTerminal` checks is not yet up to date (that's handled inside UpdatePod / syncPod). In general, the pod worker is the one who should be managing shutdown. We added optimizations to dispatchWork to skip the pod worker, and we historically had a race condition where the pod worker was shut down too early and thus termination never happened, but the right thing to do is to stop trying to optimize the pod worker knowing the state of the pod (it's job is to sync the pod) and instead make sure that a) the pod worker is running until a pod is deleted from api (which should be true today) and b) if we need to reduce latency of shutdown, we should do so by ensuring the pod worker gets that update. The failures here are a significant violation of our performance goals around pods, and our e2e tests are demonstrating the failures pretty cleanly, so we need to put this race condition to bed. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102025 can trigger the issue trivially, so for now using that to debug failure reasons.
root_cause: due to races between sources of truth. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102025#issuecomment-843622820 stops e2e tests from "cheating" and bypassing kubelet shutdown, and as a result some tests fail predictably (garbage collection lots of short running pods for testing various behaviors). The linked comment shows a pod that is racing between container start and pod delete. The problem is that dispatchWork invokes `podAndContainersAreTerminal()` on the containerstart event, but the cache that `podAndContainersAreTerminal` checks is not yet up to date (that's handled inside UpdatePod / syncPod).

If resource cannot be deleted in pkg, it shall not be created.
