symptoms: I investigated an issue with etcd storage metrics collection where etcd overrides weren't appearing correctly in the metrics. Expected behavior: According to the ([implementation](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L331)) and ([original intention](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118812#discussion_r1252695238)), etcd overrides should be configured separately and displayed as etcd-1, etcd-2, etc. Actual behavior: Only etcd-0 (the base etcd server) appeared in metrics, even when overrides were configured. Likely Root cause: The monitor getter (which retrieves etcd configs) is set twice: First by DefaultStorageFactory (includes overrides map) Then by SimpleStorageFactory (excludes overrides map) Since the monitor getter is a global variable, the second call overwrites the first. All subsequent monitor retrievals use SimpleStorageFactory's configuration, which lacks the etcd overrides. I was able to solve this in local testing by restricting monitor getter updates to only DefaultStorageFactory (used by the main kube-apiserver with overrides). Preventing SimpleStorageFactory from overwriting it. symptoms: When modifying static pod manifests on disk (e.g., adding `--encryption-provider-config` to kube-apiserver), the kubelet: 1. Detects the file change via inotify ✅ 2. Reads the new spec from disk ✅ 3. `podsDifferSemantically()` detects the spec changed ✅ 4. Pod workers receive the update and call `SyncPod()` ✅ 5. `computePodActions()` calls `containerChanged()` → returns **false** ❌ 6. **No container restart occurs — old configuration persists** ❌ **Impact:** This prevents any post-deployment static pod configuration changes that don't involve an image change. Specifically tested and confirmed broken: - Adding `--encryption-provider-config` flag (encryption at rest) - Adding `volumeMounts` and `volumes` - Any command-line flag additions/changes Tested on **6 control plane nodes** across **2 independent clusters** (SIT and UAT), all running Kubernetes v1.33.3 with kubeadm.
root_cause: caused by the **backup file confounding factor** (#136962) — which we've since confirmed and filed separately. Once we removed backup files and changed the image (which we thought was the workaround), the encryption config worked — but the image change may have been coincidental rather than causal. I'll reproduce the test in kind with v1.33.3 to verify, and if it works (which I now expect it will), I'll close this issue.

title: DeepDerivative silently ignores trailing slice item removals
summary: `equality.Semantic.DeepDerivative()` in `k8s.io/apimachinery` does not detect when items are removed from the end of a slice. It only compares up to `len(a)` items (the "desired" side), so any extra trailing items in `b` (the "existing" side) are silently ignored. This means if a controller uses `DeepDerivative` to determine whether an object needs updating, removing items from the end of a slice (e.g., container args, env vars, volume mounts) will never trigger an update.
symptoms: `equality.Semantic.DeepDerivative()` in `k8s.io/apimachinery` does not detect when items are removed from the end of a slice. It only compares up to `len(a)` items (the "desired" side), so any extra trailing items in `b` (the "existing" side) are silently ignored. This means if a controller uses `DeepDerivative` to determine whether an object needs updating, removing items from the end of a slice (e.g., container args, env vars, volume mounts) will never trigger an update.
root_cause: In `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/conversion/equalities.go`, the `deepDerivative` method has this logic for slices: ```go for i := range a { // iterates only up to len(a) if !e.deepDerivative(a[i], b[i]) { return false } } return true ``` It iterates only over the indices of \`a\` (desired). If \`a\` has 2 items and \`b\` has 3, the third item in \`b\` is never examined.

title: [Scheduling] OpportunisticBatching: redundant synchronous RunFilterPlugins call in batchStateCompatible for low-resource pods
summary: When OpportunisticBatching (KEP-5598) is enabled, `batchStateCompatible` performs a synchronous `RunFilterPlugins` call on the `lastChosenNode` to validate whether the cached batch state is still usable (i.e., the previously chosen node is now full). For pods with low resource requirements that do not fill up a node, this check always passes (not rejected), causing `batchStateCompatible` to always return `false`. This means: 1. **The synchronous `RunFilterPlugins` call is pure overhead** — it r…
symptoms: When OpportunisticBatching (KEP-5598) is enabled, `batchStateCompatible` performs a synchronous `RunFilterPlugins` call on the `lastChosenNode` to validate whether the cached batch state is still usable (i.e., the previously chosen node is now full). For pods with low resource requirements that do not fill up a node, this check always passes (not rejected), causing `batchStateCompatible` to always return `false`. This means: 1. **The synchronous `RunFilterPlugins` call is pure overhead** — it runs on the critical scheduling path, adds latency, and never yields a useful result for these pods. 2. **The same node is filtered twice** — once synchronously in `batchStateCompatible`, and again in the parallel `findNodesThatPassFilters` pipeline (since `lastChosenNode` is part of `allNodes`). 3. **The batch cache is flushed every cycle** — preventing any future batching even though the pod signatures match. This is a common scenario in production clusters with many small pods (microservices, batch workloads, etc.), where the batching optimization provides no benefit but introduces consistent per-cycle overhead.
root_cause: caused by candidate-subset changes, and in turn allow some plugins with `NormalizeScore` to support `SignPod` as well. It should also improve performance.

title: Eviction signal is not hugepages aware
summary: On nodes with hugepages configured, the kubelet's memory.available eviction signal overstates real available regular memory by the total hugepage reservation. This causes eviction to fire later than the configured threshold intends, causing OOM kills. The root cause is that AvailableBytes is computed as root_cgroup.memory.limit - root_cgroup.memory.workingSet, where: - memory.limit is set to MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (includes hugepage-reserved RAM) - memory.workingSet comes from the memory c…
symptoms: On nodes with hugepages configured, the kubelet's memory.available eviction signal overstates real available regular memory by the total hugepage reservation. This causes eviction to fire later than the configured threshold intends, causing OOM kills. The root cause is that AvailableBytes is computed as root_cgroup.memory.limit - root_cgroup.memory.workingSet, where: - memory.limit is set to MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (includes hugepage-reserved RAM) - memory.workingSet comes from the memory cgroup controller (does not track hugetlb allocations — those use a separate controller) This creates "phantom" available bytes equal to the hugepage reservation. The kernel's own MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo does not have this problem because hugepage-reserved pages are removed from the buddy allocator's free pool at boot and never appear in MemFree.
root_cause: that AvailableBytes is computed as root_cgroup.memory.limit - root_cgroup.memory.workingSet, where: - memory.limit is set to MemTotal from /proc/meminfo (includes hugepage-reserved RAM) - memory.workingSet comes from the memory cgroup controller (does not track hugetlb allocations — those use a separate controller) This creates "phantom" available bytes equal to the hugepage reservation. The kernel's own MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo does not have this problem because hugepage-reserved pages are removed from the buddy allocator's free pool at boot and never appear in MemFree.

title: Kubelet can leave projected service account token expired after transient TokenRequest/NodeAuthorizer failures during control-plane restart
summary: After upgrading a Talos Kubernetes cluster from v1.35 to v1.36, some running pods stopped receiving projected service account token rotations. The affected pods were not terminating. During the control-plane restart window, kubelet logged transient TokenRequest / NodeAuthorizer failures like: `Error preparing data for projected volume sa-token for pod network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm: failed to fetch token: serviceaccounts "external" is forbidden: User "system:node:k8s-1" cannot create resourc…
symptoms: After upgrading a Talos Kubernetes cluster from v1.35 to v1.36, some running pods stopped receiving projected service account token rotations. The affected pods were not terminating. During the control-plane restart window, kubelet logged transient TokenRequest / NodeAuthorizer failures like: `Error preparing data for projected volume sa-token for pod network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm: failed to fetch token: serviceaccounts "external" is forbidden: User "system:node:k8s-1" cannot create resource "serviceaccounts/token" in API group "" in the namespace "network": no relationship found between node 'k8s-1' and this object` There were also kubelet TokenRequest EOFs against the local API endpoint: `Couldn't update token: Post "https://127.0.0.1:7445/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/serviceaccounts/default/token": EOF` After the API server became healthy again, the projected token files stayed stale for hours. Example affected pod: pod: network/external-5f8b6fdd5c-g4vzm node: k8s-1 token iat: 2026-04-28T20:46:41Z token exp: 2026-04-28T21:46:41Z projected volume symlink stayed at: ..2026_04_28_20_46_41... A second pod on another node had a token issued at 2026-04-28T20:52:02Z, expiring at 2026-04-28T21:52:02Z, and also remained frozen at that timestamp. The application impact was Envoy Gateway data-plane pods failing xDS authentication after token expiry: `failed to validate token {"error": "token review found error: [invalid bearer token, service account token has expired]"}` Because the Envoy data-plane could not reconnect to xDS, it kept stale endpoint config until the pods were restarted.
root_cause: caused by using bind instead of rbind for mounting /var/lib/kubelet into kubelet container. Reported here: https://github.com/siderolabs/talos/issues/13352

title: Pod can become ignored by the scheduling queue when unlikely timing happens
summary: When pod is re-added to the scheduling queue after a failed binding cycle, the queue's Pop can be passively waiting for any pod to be added to the activeQ (and backoffQ when SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ is enabled). When an unlikely timing happens, the pod can be popped from the scheduling queue after its re-added ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/661b086ee0d115150cb222694b44b103c88a3a5d/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L887)), but before the `Done` is called for…
symptoms: When pod is re-added to the scheduling queue after a failed binding cycle, the queue's Pop can be passively waiting for any pod to be added to the activeQ (and backoffQ when SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ is enabled). When an unlikely timing happens, the pod can be popped from the scheduling queue after its re-added ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/661b086ee0d115150cb222694b44b103c88a3a5d/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L887)), but before the `Done` is called for this pod ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/661b086ee0d115150cb222694b44b103c88a3a5d/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L845)). In such case, the pod is dropped from the scheduling queue completely: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/661b086ee0d115150cb222694b44b103c88a3a5d/pkg/scheduler/backend/queue/active_queue.go#L267-L269 /sig scheduling
root_cause: that `Done()` is deferred to the end of `AddUnschedulablePodIfNotPresent`, but the broadcast that wakes waiting `Pop` callers fires before that deferred call. A `Pop` goroutine can therefore acquire `aq.lock` in the window between the broadcast and `Done()`, find the pod UID still present in `inFlightPods`, and have `unlockedMoveEntityToInFlight` silently discard it. The fix mirrors the ordering already applied for pod group members in the same function: call `Done()` after `determineSchedulingHintForInFlightPod` (which still needs the pod in `inFlightPods`) but before `requeueEntityWithQueueingStrategy` (which triggers the broadcast).

title: All containers of pod is down，but one of them in resource object is still "ready"
summary: All the readiness probes for the containers in the pod have failed, but one container in the resource object still shows a ready state.
symptoms: All the readiness probes for the containers in the pod have failed, but one container in the resource object still shows a ready state.
root_cause: caused by the following operation sequence: 1. The pod worker obtains the latest status of pod 1 from statusManager in the (*Kubelet).SyncPod method and updates some values. 2. The readiness probe of a container in pod 1 fails. The sync loop goroutine calls statusManager.SetContainerReadiness to update the readiness status of the container to false. 3. The pod worker calls statusManager.SetPodStatus to overwrite the status updated in step 2.

title: Job controller manageJob() returns active=0 during backoff, causing "cannot set more ready pods than active" status update rejection
summary: When the Job controller's `manageJob()` function determines that replacement pods are needed but a backoff timer is active (due to recent pod failures), it returns `active=0` to the caller. The caller uses this value to set `job.Status.Active=0` in a status update, while `job.Status.Ready` retains the real informer-computed count. The apiserver validation `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` (GA in 1.33 via `JobManagedBy`) correctly rejects this inconsistent update with 422. Because the status updat…
symptoms: When the Job controller's `manageJob()` function determines that replacement pods are needed but a backoff timer is active (due to recent pod failures), it returns `active=0` to the caller. The caller uses this value to set `job.Status.Active=0` in a status update, while `job.Status.Ready` retains the real informer-computed count. The apiserver validation `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` (GA in 1.33 via `JobManagedBy`) correctly rejects this inconsistent update with 422. Because the status update fails, the controller cannot: - Flush `uncountedTerminatedPods` - Remove `batch.kubernetes.io/job-tracking` finalizers from terminated pods This causes pods to appear stuck in Terminating state and job status to become stale. **Root cause:** Two locations in `manageJob()` return a hardcoded `0` instead of the real `active` count when backoff is active: ```go // Location 1: global backoff if remainingTime > 0 { jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime) return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil // BUG: should be `active` } // Location 2: per-index backoff if remainingTime > 0 { jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime) return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil // BUG: should be `active` } ``` The caller sets `job.Status.Active = active` (the returned 0), while `job.Status.Ready` stays at the informer count (e.g., 5). Result: `5 > 0` → 422. The `0` was likely a "don't care" value from before `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` validation existed. Every other return path in `manageJob` returns the real active count.
root_cause: Two locations in `manageJob()` return a hardcoded `0` instead of the real `active` count when backoff is active: ```go // Location 1: global backoff if remainingTime > 0 { jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime) return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil // BUG: should be `active` }

summary: Our production clusters run kube-proxy in `ipvs` mode. We evaluated migrating to `nftables` mode and observed that `kube-proxy` takes a long time to complete a sync, with the `nft` process at 100% CPU for most of that time. This looks related to [#135639](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135639), which was addressed in v1.36. We are testing on v1.36.1 and still see multi-minute syncs. The two dominant costs we measure are: 1. the `ListAll` (`nft --json --terse list table ip kube-…
symptoms: Our production clusters run kube-proxy in `ipvs` mode. We evaluated migrating to `nftables` mode and observed that `kube-proxy` takes a long time to complete a sync, with the `nft` process at 100% CPU for most of that time. This looks related to [#135639](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135639), which was addressed in v1.36. We are testing on v1.36.1 and still see multi-minute syncs. The two dominant costs we measure are: 1. the `ListAll` (`nft --json --terse list table ip kube-proxy`) that runs on every sync, including incremental syncs, and 1. the full sync re-emitting the entire table even when almost nothing changed.
root_cause: - `ListAll` is used to discover existing service chains and affinity sets for cleanup. - kube-proxy already keeps committed map/set element state in memory across successful syncs, but it did not keep equivalent committed state for service chains / affinity sets, so it had to rediscover the whole table every time. Draft fix approach in #139531: - Keep full sync behavior unchanged: full sync still calls `ListAll` and reconciles against nftables state. - Track committed service chains and affinity sets after successful syncs. - On incremental syncs, use that committed in-memory state for cleanup instead of calling `ListAll`. - Add a fake nftables regression test that verifies the initial full sync calls `ListAll` once and a following incremental sync skips it.

summary: During HNS restart stress scenarios combined with rapid pod scale operations, Windows KubeProxy intermittently fails to recreate LoadBalancers and logs the following error: ``` hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: Cannot create a file when that file already exists. (0xb7) ``` While HNS was temporarily unavailable, KubeProxy attempted to reconcile proxy rules. During this window: - GetHNSNetwork failed because HNS was down. - KubeProxy proceeded with LoadBalancer cleanup logic. - GetLoadBalanc…
symptoms: During HNS restart stress scenarios combined with rapid pod scale operations, Windows KubeProxy intermittently fails to recreate LoadBalancers and logs the following error: ``` hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: Cannot create a file when that file already exists. (0xb7) ``` While HNS was temporarily unavailable, KubeProxy attempted to reconcile proxy rules. During this window: - GetHNSNetwork failed because HNS was down. - KubeProxy proceeded with LoadBalancer cleanup logic. - GetLoadBalancer calls also failed due to HNS unavailability. - KubeProxy incorrectly interpreted these failures as the LoadBalancer being absent and reset the internal LoadBalancer ID/state. However, the actual HNS LoadBalancer objects were never deleted. After HNS restarted, the LoadBalancers were restored through the HNS backup/restore (rehydration) mechanism. Later, when KubeProxy attempted to recreate the same LoadBalancer/frontend configuration, the operation failed because the LoadBalancer already existed in HNS.
root_cause: The issue appears to be caused by a race between: - HNS availability during restart/recovery, and - KubeProxy reconciliation logic.

title: kubelet logs --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys) to runtime logs
summary: When kubelet is configured with `--manifest-url` and credential-bearing `--manifest-url-header` values (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values are written to kubelet runtime logs at startup, in cleartext. At static-pod source init, `makePodSourceConfig` copies the config map into a plain `http.Header` and logs it directly: ```go // pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:372-393 manifestURLHeader := make(http.Header) if len(kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader) > 0 { for k, v := range kube…
symptoms: When kubelet is configured with `--manifest-url` and credential-bearing `--manifest-url-header` values (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values are written to kubelet runtime logs at startup, in cleartext. At static-pod source init, `makePodSourceConfig` copies the config map into a plain `http.Header` and logs it directly: ```go // pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:372-393 manifestURLHeader := make(http.Header) if len(kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader) > 0 { for k, v := range kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader { for i := range v { manifestURLHeader.Add(k, v[i]) // values copied into a plain http.Header } } } ... if kubeCfg.StaticPodURL != "" { logger.Info("Adding pod URL with HTTP header", "URL", kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, "header", manifestURLHeader) // <-- sink config.NewSourceURL(logger, kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, manifestURLHeader, ...) } ``` The codebase already knows this field is secret and masks it elsewhere: ```go // pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107 StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"` ``` …and the *config-dump* path redacts it before logging the full `KubeletConfiguration` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:287-290` masks the map to `<masked>`). But `makePodSourceConfig` logs the **runtime `http.Header` copy**, not the config map — so neither the `datapolicy:"token"` tag nor the logging-mask applies, and the header values ship out verbatim. (`datapolicy` only fires on a strongly-typed field argument; here the value has been flattened into an `http.Header` passed as a generic `"header"` argument.)
root_cause: clear: `makePodSourceConfig` in `pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:372-393` copies `StaticPodURLHeader` into a plain `http.Header` and logs it via `logger.Info`, bypassing the `datapolicy:"token"` redaction that the config-dump path applies.

title: KEP-5491: `matchAttribute` constraint fails to allocate devices when backtracking is required (DRAListTypeAttributes)
summary: When using `DRAListTypeAttributes` is enabled (list-type device attributes), `matchAttribute` fails the device allcation even when a valid combination of devices exists. For example, given four devices where attributes are lists of values: - `dev1: attr=[1,2]` - `dev2: attr=[1]` - `dev3: attr=[2]` - `dev4: attr=[2]` The device allocator fails to find the valid allocation `{dev1, dev3, dev4}` because after removing `dev2` during backtracking, the intersection kept in the allocator is still `{1}`…
symptoms: When using `DRAListTypeAttributes` is enabled (list-type device attributes), `matchAttribute` fails the device allcation even when a valid combination of devices exists. For example, given four devices where attributes are lists of values: - `dev1: attr=[1,2]` - `dev2: attr=[1]` - `dev3: attr=[2]` - `dev4: attr=[2]` The device allocator fails to find the valid allocation `{dev1, dev3, dev4}` because after removing `dev2` during backtracking, the intersection kept in the allocator is still `{1}` (stale from when `dev2` was added), causing `dev3` and `dev4` to be incorrectly rejected as below: 1. Add `dev1` → intersection becomes `{1,2}` 1. Add `dev2` → intersection shrinks to `{1}` 1. Try `dev3` → `{2} ∩ {1} = ∅` → rejected 1. Try `dev4` → same rejection 1. Backtrack: remove `dev2` → only`numDevices` goes to 1, but intersection is still `{1}` (BUG) 1. Retry `dev3` → rejected (wrong! `{1,2} ∩ {2} = {2}` is valid) 1. Allocation fails despite `{dev1, dev3, dev4}` being a valid solution
root_cause: in [`matchAttributeConstraint`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L865-L878) in [the experimental allocator](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go). The allocator uses recursive depth-first search with backtracking. When a device is tentatively added to the `matchAttributeConstarint`, [`add()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L880) narrows the intersection to the running intersection of all device attribute sets. However, when the allocator backtracks and calls [`remove()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L965), the intersection is _never_ restored. Subsequent candidates are then evaluated against a stale, over-restricted intersection and incorrectly rejected.

title: When a node restarts, only the first init container is executed.
summary: Our pod has two init containers. After the node restarted, the first init container ran again, but the second init container did not execute, and the main container started running. The reason is that when the power is cut off, all init containers have been successfully executed, the main container has been created, but it is not running and remains in the create state. ``` [root@taocanmaster1host ~]# crictl ps -a | grep node-ag c184da0ba17b5 cd62784d2eb2b 4 days ago Running agent 1 81af3eb5688…
symptoms: Our pod has two init containers. After the node restarted, the first init container ran again, but the second init container did not execute, and the main container started running. The reason is that when the power is cut off, all init containers have been successfully executed, the main container has been created, but it is not running and remains in the create state. ``` [root@taocanmaster1host ~]# crictl ps -a | grep node-ag c184da0ba17b5 cd62784d2eb2b 4 days ago Running agent 1 81af3eb568823 agent-g6hzd ee5aef279cc06 cd62784d2eb2b 4 days ago Created agent 0 33cfe0399befe agent-g6hzd ``` According to the code, after the node is restarted, the sandbox is re-created. In this case, the first init container is directly started. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1064-L1071 When entering computePodActions for the second time, there was an issue when calculating which init container needs to be started. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L1017-L1052 As shown in the preceding figure, the computeInitContainerActions method first checks the container status. If the container is in the created or running state, the pod is considered to have been initialized. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L1083-L1087 Here, it is considered that initialization has already been completed, and subsequent operations will not be executed, causing other init containers to not execute.I think this is a bug.
root_cause: different: #137710 - purgeInitContainers fails to clean up a stale container, and that leftover is what throws things off.

title: kubelet: DRA health watch error-spams every 5s for drivers that don't implement DRAResourceHealth (Unimplemented not handled)
summary: With the `ResourceHealthStatus` feature gate (beta, on by default since 1.36), the kubelet logs an `ERROR` every 5 seconds, per DRA driver, for every driver that does not implement the optional `DRAResourceHealth` gRPC service: ``` E0709 17:55:32.410673 kubelet manager.go:1038] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="gpu.nvidia.com" E0709 17:55:3…
symptoms: With the `ResourceHealthStatus` feature gate (beta, on by default since 1.36), the kubelet logs an `ERROR` every 5 seconds, per DRA driver, for every driver that does not implement the optional `DRAResourceHealth` gRPC service: ``` E0709 17:55:32.410673 kubelet manager.go:1038] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="gpu.nvidia.com" E0709 17:55:32.413349 kubelet manager.go:1038] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="dra.cpu" ``` I hit this while running `kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu` (`dra.cpu`) and the NVIDIA GPU driver (`gpu.nvidia.com`) on a 1.36 node; both are logged every 5s, indefinitely. On a two-driver node that is 24 `ERROR` lines per minute forever. The DRAResourceHealth kubelet gRPC API is still `v1alpha1` and driver adoption is a tracked prerequisite (#139475), so essentially every DRA driver today (NVIDIA GPU, `dra-driver-cpu`, `dranet`, ...) returns `Unimplemented` and triggers this.
root_cause: The health watch is retried on a fixed 5s period with no backoff and no handling of `Unimplemented`. `pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go` (identical on `release-1.36` and `master`): ```go wait.UntilWithContext(streamCtx, func(ctx context.Context) { logger.V(4).Info("Attempting to start WatchResources health stream") stream, err := p.NodeWatchResources(ctx) if err != nil { logger.V(3).Info("Failed to establish WatchResources stream, will retry", "err", err) return } logger.V(2).Info("Successfully started WatchResources health stream") err = pm.streamHandler.HandleWatchResourcesStream(ctx, stream, driverName) logger.V(2).Info("WatchResources health stream has ended", "error", err) }, 5*time.Second) ``` `NodeWatchResources` creates the gRPC stream lazily and returns no error, so the code reaches `HandleWatchResourcesStream`, where the first `Recv()` returns `Unimplemented`. `pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go` treats it as an unexpected error: ```go resp, err := stream.Recv() if err != nil { if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) || errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) { ...; return err } if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) { ...; return nil } // Other errors are unexpected, log & return. logger.Error(err, "Error receiving from WatchResources stream") // Unimplemented lands here return err } ``` `wait.UntilWithContext(..., 5*time.Second)` ignores the returned error and re-runs the whole thing 5s later, so the `Unimplemented` is re-hit and re-logged at `ERROR` forever. At default…

title: kube-controller-manager panics (nil pointer dereference) when a StorageVersionMigration targets a resource not present in the RESTMapper
summary: Creating a `StorageVersionMigration` for a resource, then removing that resource from the cluster (e.g. deleting the CRD) while the migration is still pending, makes the `kube-controller-manager` panic and enter `CrashLoopBackOff`. The storage-version-migrator controller's `sync` dereferences a nil `*schema.GroupVersionResource`: ``` E0714 13:08:33 "Observed a panic" panic="runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference" k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator.…
symptoms: Creating a `StorageVersionMigration` for a resource, then removing that resource from the cluster (e.g. deleting the CRD) while the migration is still pending, makes the `kube-controller-manager` panic and enter `CrashLoopBackOff`. The storage-version-migrator controller's `sync` dereferences a nil `*schema.GroupVersionResource`: ``` E0714 13:08:33 "Observed a panic" panic="runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference" k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator.(*SVMController).sync(...) pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator/storageversionmigrator.go:227 ... panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked] ``` In `sync`, `resourceFor` returns `(nil, false, nil)` when the resource is not in the RESTMapper (this is the normal "unknown resource" return, not an error), and the following line logs `gvr.String()` on that nil pointer: ```go gvr, exists, err := resourceFor(svmc.restMapper, toBeProcessedSVM.Spec.Resource) if err != nil { return err } if !exists { logger.V(4).Info("resource does not exist in our rest mapper", "gvr", gvr.String()) // gvr is nil -> panic ... } ``` `GroupVersionResource.String()` has a value receiver, so calling it on a nil pointer dereferences it. The arguments of `logger.V(4).Info(...)` are evaluated unconditionally, so this happens regardless of the log verbosity. The panic crashes the whole controller-manager (all controllers stop) until the offending `StorageVersionMigration` is removed. Note: the sibling function in the same package (`ResourceVersionController.sync` in `resourceversion.go`) handles the exact same `!exists` case without touching `gvr`, which is what makes this look like an oversight.
root_cause: a single line (`gvr.String()` on a nil pointer). Trigger requires cluster-admin rights (StorageVersionMigration is cluster-scoped) plus the target resource disappearing from the RESTMapper, so this is not a privilege-escalation issue, but the crash takes down the entire controller-manager. I have a fix ready (a one-line change: log the migration's `spec.resource` instead of the nil `gvr`) plus a regression test that panics without the fix and passes with it, and I'm happy to open a PR.

title: CPUManager distribute-cpus-across-cores relies on CPU numbering order instead of topology
summary: The `distribute-cpus-across-cores` CPU manager policy option (KEP-4176, alpha since v1.31) does not correctly spread CPUs across physical cores on systems where sibling thread CPU IDs are contiguous (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3). The spread algorithm in `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` sorts CPUs numerically within each socket: ```go func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int { var result []int for _, socket := range a.sortAvailableSockets() { cpus := a.details.CPUsInSoc…
symptoms: The `distribute-cpus-across-cores` CPU manager policy option (KEP-4176, alpha since v1.31) does not correctly spread CPUs across physical cores on systems where sibling thread CPU IDs are contiguous (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3). The spread algorithm in `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` sorts CPUs numerically within each socket: ```go func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int { var result []int for _, socket := range a.sortAvailableSockets() { cpus := a.details.CPUsInSockets(socket).UnsortedList() sort.Ints(cpus) result = append(result, cpus...) } return result } ``` This assumes that numerically-sorted CPU IDs naturally interleave across physical cores. That assumption holds on systems where the BIOS/firmware enumerates all first threads before second threads (e.g., core 0 thread 0 = CPU 0, core 1 thread 0 = CPU 1, ..., core 0 thread 1 = CPU 8, core 1 thread 1 = CPU 9), but fails when sibling threads have contiguous IDs (e.g., core 0 = CPUs 0,1; core 1 = CPUs 2,3). With contiguous siblings, `sortAvailableCPUsSpread()` produces the same CPU order as `sortAvailableCPUsPacked()`, and the spreading has no effect — both allocate sibling threads together.
root_cause: The algorithm uses `sort.Ints()` on CPU IDs as a proxy for topology-aware spreading. It should instead use the core topology information already available in `cpuAccumulator.details` to explicitly round-robin across cores: ```go func (a *cpuAccumulator) sortAvailableCPUsSpread() []int { var result []int coresCPUs := make(map[int][]int) maxThreads := 0 for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() { cpus := a.details.CPUsInCores(core).SortedList() coresCPUs[core] = cpus if len(cpus) > maxThreads { maxThreads = len(cpus) } } // Round-robin: pick thread 0 from all cores, then thread 1, etc. for t := 0; t < maxThreads; t++ { for _, core := range a.sortAvailableCores() { if t < len(coresCPUs[core]) { result = append(result, coresCPUs[core][t]) } } } return result } ``` This approach works regardless of CPU numbering because it explicitly iterates cores and picks one thread per core before doubling up.

title: kubelet copies IPv6 link-local scoped nameservers from the node resolv.conf into pods where they cannot work
summary: With `dnsPolicy: Default`, kubelet copies the node resolv.conf nameservers into the pod verbatim. When the node file contains an IPv6 link-local nameserver with a scope zone, for example `nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3`, that exact line is written into the pod `/etc/resolv.conf`. symptoms: With `dnsPolicy: Default`, kubelet copies the node resolv.conf nameservers into the pod verbatim. When the node file contains an IPv6 link-local nameserver with a scope zone, for example `nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3`, that exact line is written into the pod `/etc/resolv.conf`. The scope zone is a node interface index. It does not exist in the pod network namespace, so the resolver cannot use the address (socket setup fails with `EINVAL`). This also affects CoreDNS, which runs with `dnsPolicy: Default`, inherits the same file, and forwards to it via `forward . /etc/resolv.conf`. Because the forward plugin distributes across all listed nameservers with the default random policy, a fraction of upstream lookups select the unusable server and fail intermittently with resolution timeouts. Root cause is in `parseResolvConf` (`pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go`). The nameserver value is appended verbatim with no IP parse, address family, scope, or reachability check. The only later processing is truncation to `MaxDNSNameservers` and dedup: ```go if fields[0] == "nameserver" { if len(fields) >= 2 { nameservers = append(nameservers, fields[1]) } } ```
root_cause: in `parseResolvConf` (`pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go`). The nameserver value is appended verbatim with no IP parse, address family, scope, or reachability check. The only later processing is truncation to `MaxDNSNameservers` and dedup: ```go if fields[0] == "nameserver" { if len(fields) >= 2 { nameservers = append(nameservers, fields[1]) } } ```

title: kubectl create ingress accepts trailing data in --rule and silently drops TLS
summary: kubectl create ingress accepts malformed trailing data in --rule. For example, this malformed rule passes client-side validation: foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage The extra ,garbage causes TLS parsing to be skipped. The resulting Ingress has no spec.tls, despite the rule containing tls=secret123. This is a client-side validation bug that can silently create an Ingress without the intended TLS configuration. ### What did you expect to happen? The command should reject the rule because it…
symptoms: kubectl create ingress accepts malformed trailing data in --rule. For example, this malformed rule passes client-side validation: foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage The extra ,garbage causes TLS parsing to be skipped. The resulting Ingress has no spec.tls, despite the rule containing tls=secret123. This is a client-side validation bug that can silently create an Ingress without the intended TLS configuration. ### What did you expect to happen? The command should reject the rule because it does not match the documented format: host/path=svcname:svcport[,tls[=secret]] For example: rule foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage is invalid and should be in format host/path=svcname:svcport[,tls[=secret]] ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Run: $ kubectl create ingress demo \ --rule='foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage' \ --dry-run=client \ -o yaml Expected: the command rejects the malformed rule. Actual: the command accepts it and renders an Ingress with an HTTP rule but without a spec.tls entry. The behavior was also reproduced with a focused unit test: CreateIngressOptions{ Rules: []string{"foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage"}, }.Validate() Validate() returns nil. Constructing the Ingress from those options produces zero TLS rules. ### Anything else we need to know?
root_cause: - ruleRegex is anchored at the start but not at the end. - Validate() uses MatchString, so a valid prefix is sufficient. - buildTLSRules() only processes rules split into exactly two comma-separated fields. The trailing field makes the length three, so TLS is skipped. Relevant code: - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L49 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L223 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L326 Suggested fix: end-anchor the validation regex and add regression tests for trailing data. I searched open and closed Kubernetes issues and PRs using command-, symptom-, and file-based queries and did not find an existing matching report or open fix. ### Kubernetes version Client Version: v1.36.2 Source tag commit: 24e2b02af5543d7910c2bb074c7264df5a8f0467 ### Cloud provider Not applicable. This is a client-side kubectl parsing and validation issue; it does not require a cluster or cloud provider. ### OS version Windows, amd64 ### Install tools Built/tested from a local Kubernetes source checkout with Go 1.26.4. ### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable) Not applicable. ### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable) Not applicable.

title: PodTopologySpread silently ignores the constraint when `labelSelector` is an empty (non-nil) object `{}`
summary: When a `topologySpreadConstraint` is written with an **empty but non-nil** label selector (`labelSelector: {}`), the constraint is silently treated as a no-op. `maxSkew` and `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` have no effect at all: pods are placed as if the constraint were absent, with no error, event, or warning. The root cause is a short-circuit in `countPodsMatchSelector` (`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/podtopologyspread/common.go`), introduced by commit `3dae9ba6d68` ("Optimize topology s…
symptoms: When a `topologySpreadConstraint` is written with an **empty but non-nil** label selector (`labelSelector: {}`), the constraint is silently treated as a no-op. `maxSkew` and `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` have no effect at all: pods are placed as if the constraint were absent, with no error, event, or warning. The root cause is a short-circuit in `countPodsMatchSelector` (`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/podtopologyspread/common.go`), introduced by commit `3dae9ba6d68` ("Optimize topology spreading for null selector"): ```go func countPodsMatchSelector(podInfos []fwk.PodInfo, selector labels.Selector, ns string) int { if selector.Empty() { // <-- wrong predicate return 0 } ... } ``` `selector.Empty()` reports whether the selector **has any requirements**, not whether it **matches anything**. For the two degenerate selectors these two notions are exactly inverted. The divergence originates in `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector`, which distinguishes a nil pointer (field unset) from a non-nil empty object by design: ```go func LabelSelectorAsSelector(ps *LabelSelector) (labels.Selector, error) { if ps == nil { return labels.Nothing(), nil // field unset -> match nothing } if len(ps.MatchLabels)+len(ps.MatchExpressions) == 0 { return labels.Everything(), nil // {} : no filter -> match everything } ... } ```
root_cause: a short-circuit in `countPodsMatchSelector` (`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/podtopologyspread/common.go`), introduced by commit `3dae9ba6d68` ("Optimize topology spreading for null selector"): ```go func countPodsMatchSelector(podInfos []fwk.PodInfo, selector labels.Selector, ns string) int { if selector.Empty() { // <-- wrong predicate return 0 } ... } ```

title: DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate overlong rolling-update service socket paths
summary: On current Kubernetes master, the DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate an unusable automatic service socket endpoint when rolling updates are enabled with a valid long driver name. With normal defaults: ```text plugin directory: /var/lib/kubelet/plugins/<driver name> rolling service socket: dra-<Pod UID>.sock ``` With a normal 36-byte Pod UID: ```text full endpoint length = 71 + len(driverName) ``` A valid 37-byte driver name: ```text abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io ``` produces exactly…
symptoms: On current Kubernetes master, the DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate an unusable automatic service socket endpoint when rolling updates are enabled with a valid long driver name. With normal defaults: ```text plugin directory: /var/lib/kubelet/plugins/<driver name> rolling service socket: dra-<Pod UID>.sock ``` With a normal 36-byte Pod UID: ```text full endpoint length = 71 + len(driverName) ``` A valid 37-byte driver name: ```text abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io ``` produces exactly a 108-byte endpoint under the affected implementation. Kubernetes requires AF_UNIX pathname-based endpoints to remain shorter than 108 bytes. A valid 63-byte driver name produces a 134-byte old-style endpoint.
root_cause: Rolling-update service socket naming includes the complete Pod UID. The default containing directory independently contains the complete driver name. The service socket did not check the combined full-path budget or fall back to a shorter basename.

title: kubelet: containerLogs returns HTTP 200 when the container is gone from the runtime
summary: When a container has been removed from the runtime but its Pod still exists, the kubelet /containerLogs endpoint can return HTTP 200 with the error message in the response body. kubectl logs then prints the error as if it were log output and exits 0, so clients cannot tell that the log fetch failed. The root cause is an unconditional zero-byte Write() in GetKubeletContainerLogs, which is used to flush headers early for streaming logs. net/http commits the response as 200 on the first write, so…
symptoms: When a container has been removed from the runtime but its Pod still exists, the kubelet /containerLogs endpoint can return HTTP 200 with the error message in the response body. kubectl logs then prints the error as if it were log output and exits 0, so clients cannot tell that the log fetch failed. The root cause is an unconditional zero-byte Write() in GetKubeletContainerLogs, which is used to flush headers early for streaming logs. net/http commits the response as 200 on the first write, so an error found later by ContainerStatus() cannot change the status. The affected path is getContainerLogs() → GetKubeletContainerLogs() → GetContainerLogs(), with the container lookup happening after the response has already been committed.
root_cause: an unconditional zero-byte Write() in GetKubeletContainerLogs, which is used to flush headers early for streaming logs. net/http commits the response as 200 on the first write, so an error found later by ContainerStatus() cannot change the status. The affected path is getContainerLogs() → GetKubeletContainerLogs() → GetContainerLogs(), with the container lookup happening after the response has already been committed.
